articles.title: U.S. soldier arrested in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police say
articles.summary: A member of the U.S. Army was arrested Tuesday in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police said.

image.caption: A March 2023 file shows the exterior of New Scotland Yard, the headquarters of London's Metropolitan police. A member of the U.S. Army was arrested Tuesday in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police said. (Daniel Lea/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
A member of the U.S. Army was arrested Tuesday in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police said.
Unnamed 41-year-old arrested near Gloucester

The 41-year-old, who was not named, was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of violating two sections of the U.K. National Security Act 2023 — for assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information.
The Metropolitan Police said its counterterror forces worked closely with the FBI and U.S. military.
FBI Director Kash Patel called it an "important arrest" dealing with allegations of espionage that are of "utmost concern" for the U.S. and its allies.
"This FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."
2 searches undertaken
Searches were underway at two locations in Gloucestershire, a county about 140 kilometres west of London.
The suspect was detained and in custody at a London police station.

Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterror investigations, indicating it wasn't connected with a suspected terror plot linked to Iran in September at a U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, near Gloucester.
After the threat, the U.S. Air Force withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran during the Middle East conflict from RAF Fairford.

articles.title: Thomas Markle, Meghan’s father, cut off his ankle monitor, DoJ says
articles.summary:
Estranged father of Duchess of Sussex was arrested for keeping child sexual abuse material, authorities say

The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, cut an…

blocks.text: The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, cut an electronic monitoring device off his ankle, just days after his arrest for keeping child sexual abuse material in storage units in California, authorities said on Tuesday.
Thomas Markle was in custody awaiting a hearing in federal court in Tampa, Florida, first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said.
He was arrested shortly after he cut off the ankle bracelet at 145am, Essayli said.

Markle’s arrest on Friday followed the seizure of approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images in storage in the Los Angeles area, Essayli said.

During his arrest last week, he was taken from a senior care center in Lakeland by ambulance. Hours later, a judge allowed Markle to be released on the condition that he be electronically monitored, which typically means wearing an ankle tether.
The judge also ordered a mental competency exam and a report by 20 November.

His daughter, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex married Prince Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. She is an American citizen and actor who starred in the US television drama “Suits”.

Meghan recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to police in London in 2019.

“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”
Thomas Markle was living in the Philippines this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the US.

His arrest followed reports by The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, that Meghan’s half brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. That discovery led to information about two US storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.

articles.title: More than a dozen private companies loaning workers to Major Projects Office: document
articles.summary: Private sector companies have loaned 17 employees to work at the federal Major Projects Office, according to a document provided to the House environment committee.

image.caption: Major Projects Office CEO Dawn Farrell listens as Prime Minister Mark Carney makes an announcement last year. Private sector energy and railway companies, as well as major banks, have loaned employees to the office. (Amber Bracken/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Private sector companies have loaned 17 employees to work at the federal Major Projects Office, according to a document provided to the House environment committee.
MPO set up to approve speedy construction of projects deemed in national interest
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 10, 2026 3:03 PM EST | Last Updated: 25 minutes ago
The employees come from various positions at banks, railways and energy companies, according to the document — a copy of which CBC News has obtained. The Toronto Star first reported the news.

The MPO, a key policy proposal from Prime Minister Mark Carney, was established to speed up permitting for projects considered in the national interest. A handful of projects have already been referred to the MPO, including a new oil pipeline from Alberta to the West Coast.
In addition to the 17 workers from the private sector, two dozen MPO employees have been seconded from other institutions, including federal departments and provincial and territorial governments.

Seconding employees from various institutions into federal organizations isn't a new exercise. But a briefing note obtained by CBC News indicates that "participating companies will cover 100 per cent of their employees' salaries and benefits" while they're working with the MPO.
Pacific Link pipeline listed as 'project of national interest,' says Carney
Four seconded employees come from three large banks: Scotiabank, Bank of Montreal and Royal Bank of Canada. CN Rail and CPKC railway have loaned one employee each to the MPO.
The list also includes businesses from the energy sector, including ATCO EnPower, TC Energy and TransAlta.

Pembina Pipeline Corporation, which currently owns a 10 per cent stake in the West Coast oil pipeline project, has also loaned one worker to the MPO. No company has loaned more than two employees, the document says.
Conservatives raise questions about conflict of interest

The involvement of private sector workers in the MPO raised concerns among Conservative MPs who questioned CEO Dawn Farrell and Internal Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc during a parliamentary committee last week.

Both Farrell and LeBlanc said all employees seconded from the private sector were subject to government conflict of interest rules and no employee would be involved in a project that their parent company has an interest in.
But when Conservative MPs questioned whether the government should release the names of the companies, LeBlanc seemed hesitant.
"These are people who work for these institutions who decide to step up and serve their country and help build their country," LeBlanc told the committee.

"I think there's a danger in saying that company X provided employee Y. Then there will be a whole artificial, fabricated gotcha moment … I think we've got to be careful not to cast aspersions on either the companies or the individuals."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

Nvidia said on Tuesday that Wachtell attorney Joon Kim was set to lead "a thorough and independent investigation" into Jensen Huang's affair. The FBI is also conducting its own probe.

articles.title: Crypto King's alleged kidnappers’ trial hears call Aiden Pleterski made to landlord asking for $3M
articles.summary: The jury trial for three men accused of kidnapping and extorting the self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski began Tuesday in Toronto with testimony from his former landlord.

image.caption: From left to right, Rakeem Henry, Akil Heywood and Alfredo Paladino are standing trial for the alleged kidnapping and extortion of self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski in Ontario Superior Court in Toronto. (CBC and Instagram/atlanticmastoronto)

blocks.text: Toronto·New
The jury trial for three men accused of kidnapping and extorting the self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski began Tuesday in Toronto with testimony from his former landlord.
Pleterski captured talking to landlord on 911 call recording
“I’m on a phone call right now and I believe this person is being held, kidnapped,” says Sandeep Gupta to an emergency call taker in a recording of a 911 call played in Ontario Superior Court.
“He’s not a friend; he was a renter. I don’t know if you’ve heard on the news — the Crypto King?”
Akil Heywood, Alfredo Paladino and Rakeem Henry are all charged with allegedly kidnapping and extorting Pleterski over the course of three days in early December 2022.
Paladino and Henry are also charged with firearms offences, the aggravated assault of Pleterski, assaulting him with a weapon, and assault causing bodily harm over that same period.

In her opening statement to the jury, Crown prosecutor Julia De Vuono alleged the kidnapping was a result of a “dispute over money,” and that Heywood invested and lost a significant amount with Pleterski, later playing a key role in Pleterski’s bankruptcy proceeding. She also alleged Heywood was the “driving force” behind the plan to kidnap Pleterski.
Pleterski, 27, was convicted of fraud last month, but has yet to be sentenced.
Three men are standing trial for the alleged kidnapping and extortion of Aiden Pleterski in December 2022. (aiden.ptrs/Instagram)

The Crown said prosecution evidence would show another man, Deren Akyeam-Pong, who is not part of the trial, was the lead kidnapper and alleged Paladino and Henry carried out the kidnapping alongside him.

Between the initial alleged kidnapping on Dec. 5, and Pleterski’s release on Dec. 8, De Vuono said Pleterski was waterboarded, burned with cigarettes, beaten with weapons and had a gun fired beside his head twice.
'I need my money'

Gupta testified Pleterski called him several times before he finally answered after midnight, in the early hours of Dec. 6, 2022. During the call with Pleterski, Gupta said, he also called 911 on his wife’s phone and maintained conversations with both Pleterski and the 911 operator on speaker phone, so the 911 call recorded what he was saying.
Throughout the call, Pleterski makes several pleas to Gupta to get him millions of dollars.
“I need my money, I need $2 [million] to $3 million, as soon as you can, so I can pay these guys,” he says.
Gupta tries to get information about where Pleterski is throughout the call, and explains that it’s not possible to get that amount of money very quickly.

His family business had a rent-to-own agreement with Pleterski for a Burlington, Ont., home that Gupta said was worth about $10 million in 2022. But he testified that Pleterski stopped making rent payments in April 2022 and never completed the purchase.

The court is expected to hear another phone call recording this afternoon, in which Gupta testified he made a plan to meet up with Pleterski at a Tim Hortons, at the direction of police, to give him money.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: French police raid Ritz hotel in Mohamed Al Fayed sexual abuse investigation
articles.summary:
Arrests made after three properties were searched in relation to inquiry into late businessman

French police have made arrests after raiding three properties, including the

blocks.text: French police have made arrests after raiding three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, in relation to an investigation into sexual abuse and trafficking by Mohamed Al Fayed.

Several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released, according to the Paris public prosecutor’s office. Another property in Paris and one in Saint-Tropez, both with links to Fayed, were also searched in mid-October.
Several of Fayed’s alleged victims were also interviewed by officers from the organised crime division of the Paris prosecutor’s office.

It added that the searches were part of a preliminary investigation into “allegations of human trafficking committed by an organised group, aggravated pimping committed by an organised group, and rape”.

In an email sent to survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse earlier today, the Metropolitan police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in a coordinated operation with French investigators.

The Paris prosecutor’s office said: “Searches and evidence-gathering operations were carried out in mid-October 2026, notably within the Hotel Ritz in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, as well as at the Villa Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez, a former property of Mohamed Al Fayed, and at the Villa Windsor in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, in the presence of British investigators.”
The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed, it added.

One of the properties that was raided was Castel Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez is one of the most exclusive villas on the French Riviera, and where Diana, Princess of Wales, stayed with her sons in the summer of 1997, at the start of her relationship with Fayed’s son, Dodi.

The other was Villa Windsor, a former holiday home of the Fayed family. The property in western Paris was previously the family home of Charles de Gaulle, before he was president of France, and King Edward VIII, after his abdication, and his wife, Wallis Simpson.
A Met spokesperson confirmed its officers travelled to France last month and were present during the operation.
Campaign groups representing Fayed’s alleged victims called on the Met police to conduct its own searches of the late billionaire’s properties.

Co-chairs of Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors, Jen Mills and Lindsay Mason, said: “We want to see the same thoroughness applied to every property where survivors say they were taken or abused, including here in Britain. The searches in Paris and Saint-Tropez must be the beginning, not the end.”

A spokesperson for No One Above, a collective of survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse, said: “The French authorities have put this in the hands of their specialist trafficking unit and their organised crime prosecutors, and are investigating it as trafficking by an organised gang.

“The evidence in this case was never confined to Harrods. For two years, the Met has avoided treating it as what France recognised from the outset: organised trafficking by a network. The National Crime Agency should now take over the investigation.”

Pelham Spong, who says she was trafficked in Paris on Fayed’s orders in 2008 before being sent to London to be sexually assaulted by him, said she was overjoyed by the French police raids. “Survivors deserve actions, not words,” she added.

Last November, she told French investigators from the Central Office for the Repression of Human Trafficking that Fayed, who owned the Ritz hotel in Paris, had forcibly kissed her and offered her a salary of €65,000 a year if she slept with him.

Survivors’ groups say more than 500 women have come forward about abuse that allegedly took place at Harrods, Park Lane, Fulham football club, the Ritz hotel in Paris, and other places owned by Fayed. The Met is investigating 169 victims who have contacted the force directly.

The Ritz Paris told Agence France-Presse news agency that it “does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour” and that it was ready “to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities”.

articles.title: Parents sue to stop Washington state trans sports ban that could require ‘invasive’ genital exams
articles.summary:
Voters adopted extreme policy requiring medical sex verification for all girls who want to play team sports

Parents of student athletes in Washington state have sued to block a ballot…

blocks.text: Parents of student athletes in Washington state have sued to block a ballot initiative banning transgender girls from women’s sports teams, calling the measure discriminatory and warning it would lead to “invasive” genital examinations for female athletes.

Last week, voters in the solidly Democratic state passed Initiative 638, a major setback for LGBTQ+ rights amid the “blue wave” of the US midterm elections. Nebraska, Colorado and Arizona adopted similar anti-trans sports bans, though advocates say Washington state’s policy is particularly extreme due to its medical sex verification requirement for all girls who want to play team sports.

The lawsuit was filed in state court on Monday by parents of trans and cisgender girls; TransFamilies, a non-profit Washington advocacy group; and the Washington Education Association, the teachers’ union. They are represented by the American Civil Liberties Union of Washington; Legal Voice, a group that fights gender discrimination; and Pacifica Law Group, a local firm.

Washington’s measure mandates that girls provide documentation from medical providers about their sex before they join women’s teams, either through hormone or genetic tests or examinations of their “reproductive anatomy”. The policy does not apply to boys.

Doctors, teachers and parents have raised alarms about the potential of forcing girls to undergo genital exams, saying the enforcement mechanism was a severe privacy violation and would discourage all girls from joining sports. Proponents argue that the ban, funded by Brian Heywood, a conservative hedge fund manager, protects “fairness” in girls’ sports.

The law applies to students in elementary, middle and high school. School officials said earlier this year that they were aware of only about 10 trans sports players statewide, a tiny fraction of the state’s 200,000 student athletes.

The suit argues that the measure violates Washington’s constitution, including by infringing on students’ privacy and violating equal rights protections by only applying to girls. The ban also violates an anti-discrimination law that protects trans people, the suit says.

Tiffani Lennon, executive director of Legal Voice, noted that Washington state has for 20 years allowed trans youth to play on teams that match their gender: “This is a fabricated issue being manufactured to create alarm. They’re intending to send a message to trans youth that we don’t want you visible, and they are willing to put in place really extreme measures to ensure that it terrifies enough people to go run and hide.”

The plaintiffs include a parent of a 17-year-old trans girl who participates in team sports at her high school and who fears being outed and kicked out of athletics under the measure. Parents of two cisgender female athletes also joined the suit, saying they oppose the “intrusive” sex verification requirements.
“If you really want fairness in sports, why would you subject girls to sex verification? Why would you dissuade girls from participating in sports?” said Lennon. “It’s clearly discriminatory.”
On Monday, the Seattle public schools board of directors also voted in favor of allowing the district to take legal action against the ban, which is due to go into effect on 3 December.

articles.title: British counterterrorism police arrest US soldier accused of spying on behalf of Russia
articles.summary: A member of the US Army has been arrested in near Gloucester in England. Police said he was suspected of espionage activity in connection with Russia. Investigators from the US and UK are involved in…

image.caption: A series of US military and intelligence facilities and operations are based in the area around Gloucester and Cheltenham in the west of England, including but not limited to the Fairford air baseImage: Simon Chapman/London News Pictures/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A 41-year-old member of the US Army was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday in England, the Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
Authorities were searched two locations in the Gloucestershire region, police said, adding: "The country to which the allegations pertain is Russia."
US authorities, the US Military and the FBI were closely involved in the investigation, police said.
The man was in custody at a London police station, authorities said on Tuesday evening as the news emerged.
What did US and UK officials say about the arrest?

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing called it a "significant arrest" as a result of "close collaboration between UK and US authorities."
"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Evans said.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the case was of "utmost concern" to the US and its allies.

"While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message — this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners," Patel said. He also expressed thanks to UK investigators across various branches and the US Military Counterintelligence Command "for their outstanding work."
Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command also said the case demonstrated the "resolve of the counterintelligence community."
"The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent," Stinchon said.

blocks.caption: The headquarters of UK signals intelligence agency GCHQ is located not far from the site of Tuesday's arrestImage: Barry Batchelor/PA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Busy area for US and UK military, intelligence communities

The area around Gloucestershire in the west of England, around two hours' drive from London, is home to several sensitive military and intelligence sites as well as outposts for various British and US companies with ties to the defense industry.
RAF Fairford, which was in the news earlier this year amid the security scare at the vast airbase used by both UK and US planes, is not far southeast of Gloucester.
Gloucester's neighboring town, Cheltenham, is one the UK's intelligence capitals outside London, home to the headquarters of the country's signals intelligence agency GCHQ.
This is a developing story. More to follow...

articles.title: Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM's supporters stage protest
articles.summary: Supporters of Sheikh Hasina want her to return from exile in India.

blocks.text: Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.
Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.
A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.
Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.
Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.

"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.

"Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.
Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.
Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.
The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed, most by gunfire from security forces, during the anti-government protests in 2024.
The activities of the Awami League were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.
A special Bangladeshi tribunal last year sentenced her to death in absentia after being found guilty of crimes against humanity.
She has denied all the charges, calling the trial "biased and politically motivated".
Despite the death penalty threat, Hasina said she wanted to return to Bangladesh in December and requesteded the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to issue her with a passport.
But the Bangladeshi government said the country would not provide a passport to her and called her "a terrorist".
"She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign affairs minister, said.
"Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her to come and visit her in-laws' residence?" Kobir asked.
A state prosecutor in Bangladesh on Tuesday said the verdict would be executed if she came back, saying she had missed the opportunity to appeal.
Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.
Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted.

articles.title: UK counter-terrorism police arrest member of US army with alleged links to Russia
articles.summary:
Man, 41, arrested as part of an investigation by British police working with US authorities, US military and FBI

blocks.text: A US soldier with alleged links to Russia has been arrested by British counter-terrorism police
The man, 41, was arrested as part of an investigation by counter terrorism policing, working closely with US authorities, the US military and the FBI, counter terrorism policing London said.
US army counterintelligence command said the allegations related to a “senior soldier”.
The man was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday on suspicion of offences under section one and section three of the National Security Act and remains in custody at a London police station.
As part of the investigation, officers were carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan police said.
The FBI director, Kash Patel, said in a statement the arrest “involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies”.

He added: “While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.
“This includes 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests from this FBI over the last 21 months – a 53% increase.

“This matter shows that partnerships are essential to protect our countries and I want to express my thanks to UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command for their outstanding work.”
The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing counter terrorism policing investigations.
Deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said: “The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing.
“This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved.
“We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security.”

Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US army counterintelligence command, said the alleged conduct “of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent”.
He added: “I encourage anyone who thinks they’ve witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office.”

articles.title: UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law
articles.summary: A London court has overturned a Trinidad and Tobago law criminalizing consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples. As a result of the colonial legacy, it is the independent country's…

image.caption: The UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967, but similar colonial-era laws remain in place in several Caribbean nationsImage: Yui Mok/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A man from Trinidad and Tobago has won a legal appeal lasting almost a decade in the last court of appeal available to him — the judicial committee of the Privy Council in former colonial power Britain.

Jason Jones, a gay man born in Trinidad and Tobago, had challenged the Caribbean nation's Sexual Offences Act outlawing consensusal sex between adult males, saying that it breached his fundamental rights under the country's constitution.

He initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago's High Court, but the government and religious organizations managed to partially overturn the ruling once more, prompting Jones to the take the case to the island nation's highest appellate authority — the Privy Council in the UK.
"To discriminate against somebody simply because of who they choose to love is simply ridiculous," Jones told the Associated Press after Tuesday's judgment was rendered.

The Privy Council in London is the final court of appeal for some Commonwealth countries including Trinidad and Tobago, although that issue was already contentious in some circles prior to Tuesday's ruling.

blocks.caption: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories, Crown dependencies and some Commonwealth countries, including Trinidad and TobagoImage: Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did the London court rule?
A panel of five judges unanimously allowed Jones' appeal, dismissing a counter-appeal from the Caribbean country's Attorney General.

It found that two sections of the country's Sexual Offenses Act 1986, criminalizing "buggery" and "serious indecency" respectively among same-sex couples, violated Jones' fundamental rights to private and family life set out in the 1976 constitution.

The court wrote in its ruling that "the rights and interests of Mr Jones which are at stake involve a particularly important facet of his existence and identity since the ability to form an intimate and loving relationship with another person lies at the core of the right to private and family life."
The anti-gay laws that call for up to five years in prison have not been enforced in recent history, but critics say they still send an intimidating message.

Judge Philip Sales said as he announced the ruling that "the current understanding of the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one's sexual orientation."
Sales added that "laws which seek to criminalize such activities cannot be justified."

Trinidadian authorities argued that because the 1986 laws were passed with a super-majority and constituted criminal penalties that dated back to colonial times, prior to the constitution, they could be considered "existing law" and override the individual constitutional rights in certain circumstances.

But the Privy Council judges found that the so-called "proviso" for this special status — "unless the Act is shown not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual" — had not been met.
One of Jones' lawyers, Anand Ramlogan, is a former attorney general of Trinidad and Tobago and argued against this position earlier in the case.

"Constitutional rights exist precisely because majorities are not always right," Ramlogan said. "They ensure that the dignity and equality of every citizen are not left to the changing tides of public opinion."
Who is the appellant?
Jason Jones is a 61-year-old born in Trinidad and Tobago.
Openly gay since the age of 16, he said he fled the country in 1996 because of homophobic violence and discrimination.

Speaking to the Associated Press on Tuesday after what he termed a "stunning victory," he said he would describe himself as a "very angry gay man," whose anger had helped him persist in his legal appeal for so many years.

"Society has treated me worse than a criminal," he said. "There is a real sense of vindication with this judgment. Finally, the courts are seeing that they need to step up because our politicians are so toothless."

He said he became inspired to speak out after losing friends to HIV/AIDS and after meeting American singer-songwriter Nina Simone when she toured the island nation for three weeks in 1984, when he was 19.
"Nina was the one who said, 'Jason, get off this rock and go see the world,'" he said, calling it a defining and life-changing experience.
New bill in Ghana criminalizes LGBTQ+ activity
Trinidad and Tobago may not enforce its 'buggery' law, but it carries a custodial sentence

Trinidad and Tobago's government, the country's Council of Evangelical Churches and its largest Hindu organization, Sanatan Dharm Maha Sabha, contested the case, which has wound its way through several courts since the appeal was launched in 2017.

In 2018, Trinidad's High Court found the laws unconstitutional. But in 2025, a local appeals court partially reversed the ruling. Trinidad's Court of Appeals subsequently allowed Jones to seek a ruling from the final appeals court in England.
The case was being closely watched by activists across the Caribbean, with similar laws in place in several other countries in the region.
The Bahamas decriminalized homosexuality in 1991.
The UK repealed laws in overseas territories Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands in 2001.
Judges in Barbados, Dominica, St. Lucia and Antigua and Barbuda have also recently struck down similar laws.
But in former British colonies Grenada, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and St. Vincent and the Grenadines it remains a crime.

The UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967, more than four centuries after the so-called "buggery" laws were first introduced under King Henry VII, and more than a century after the last executions for the crime. People still faced prosecution or the threat of it for consensual adult gay sex until after World War II, with surely the most famous later-years case being that of computing and codebreaking pioneer and war hero Alan Turing.

articles.title: Trump’s FCC nominee avoids questions from Democrats on Carr’s ‘censorship agenda’
articles.summary:
Senators pressured Danielle Thumann, senior counsel to FCC chair Brendan Carr, to speak about agency’s actions toward ABC and Jimmy Kimmel

During a contentious Tuesday hearing on her…

blocks.text: During a contentious Tuesday hearing on her nomination by Donald Trump to serve as a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) commissioner, Senate Democrats hammered Danielle Thumann about recent actions taken by the Brendan Carr-led regulator that have been criticized as hostile to press freedom.

Thumann, who serves as senior counsel to Carr, is expected to be approved as commissioner, with Republicans in charge of the US Senate and House. But Ben Ray Luján, a senator of New Mexico, assured her that the commission’s actions will be under close scrutiny when Democrats take charge of the chamber in January.

Luján asked Thumann repeatedly whether she agrees with actions taken by Carr’s FCC, including a nearly unprecedented order in late April forcing ABC to apply early to renew its local station licenses, a move that immediately followed criticism of one of the network’s biggest stars, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, by the president and Melania Trump, the first lady. Carr was also accused of pressuring ABC affiliates to drop Kimmel’s show the previous fall.
“Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airways?” Luján asked.

“I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related issues, and I’m not familiar with all of the details regarding the investigation of ABC or the early license renewal of their licenses,” Thumann responded. “And I haven’t been involved in any of those conversations regarding any of their practices or regarding Jimmy Kimmel.”

Luján pressed Thumann to name an issue she has disagreed with Carr on, and she demurred. He also asked her whether it was “appropriate for the FCC to call up Disney’s broadcast license for early renewal”.

Several of Luján’s Democratic colleagues also took turns pressuring Thumann on the FCC’s actions toward television networks, with Ed Markey, the Massachusetts senator, grilling her on “Chairman Carr’s FCC censorship agenda”. “Ms Thumann, does the FCC have the authority to punish a broadcaster because the president disagrees with its news coverage?”

Pushing back on her response, Markey said: “Again, this should be a straightforward constitutional limitation, because the FCC cannot punish a broadcaster simply because the president doesn’t like his coverage. Yet Chairman Carr, your boss right now, has threatened to do exactly that.”

Markey accused her of choosing to “evade” his questions, saying that “anyone seeking a seat on the Federal Communications Commission must be willing to stand up to such threats and to defend the first amendment, and you are not willing to do so here in your confirmation hearing.”

Senator Tammy Duckworth also asked Thumann about whether she would yield to political pressure to punish disfavored networks. While Thumann said the commission has to deal with complaints against networks it regulates, she acknowledged that “editorial decision-making is protected by the first amendment for broadcasters”, and added: “I don’t think that a decision [about a station’s license] should be based purely on someone’s discontent with the content that’s being aired.”

Several Senate Democrats said it was inappropriate for the commerce committee to hold the confirmation hearing, and that if Republicans were going to nominate another member of the party to the commission, they should follow past precedent and nominate a Democrat as well. The FCC currently has one commissioner nominated by a Democratic president, Anna M Gomez, but her term has already technically expired.

At the end of the hearing, Luján issued a warning to Carr. “Mr Carr, if you’re listening now, know you’re going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions, and you don’t have the protection of the gavel any longer,” he said. “Subpoena authorities that you have to respond to so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place.”

articles.title: Supreme Court reserves decision on whether federal firearms ban should stand
articles.summary: The question of whether the federal government had the authority to ban hundreds of makes and models of firearms is now in the hands of the country's top court after it heard arguments from gun…

image.caption: Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada Richard Wagner speaks during a ceremony marking the opening of the judicial year of the Supreme Court of Canada, temporarily located in the West Memorial Building, in Ottawa, on Oct. 5. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The question of whether the federal government had the authority to ban hundreds of makes and models of firearms is now in the hands of the country's top court after it heard arguments from gun advocates and government lawyers.
Decision from Canada's top court not expected for a few months
The question of whether the federal government had the authority to ban hundreds of makes and models of firearms is now in the hands of the country's top court.

Over the past two days the justices of the Supreme Court of Canada have heard arguments from gun advocates and other interested parties challenging the Justin Trudeau-era policy outlawing hundreds of makes and models, including the AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14.

In 2020, the government leaned on its regulatory powers to ban the use, sale and importation of some 1,500 firearms following the Nova Scotia mass killing, the worst in modern Canadian history. The banned list has since grown to 2,500 varieties with Ottawa arguing "their inherent deadliness makes them unsuitable for civilian use and a serious threat to public safety given the degree to which they can increase the severity of mass shootings."
The 2020 regulations were challenged by licensed firearm owners, hunters, sport shooters and the Canadian Coalition for Firearm Rights — the country's gun lobby.
Previous rulings in government's favour

Their case centres on whether the government had the authority to ban guns via an order issued by Governor in Council — effectively the federal cabinet. Under the Criminal Code, the cabinet can't use regulations to outlaw a firearm if it considers that gun "reasonable for use in Canada for hunting or sporting purposes."

The government's lawyers have argued that Parliament has long empowered cabinet with broad discretionary authority to prohibit firearms in the interest of public safety and that there are other non-prohibited firearms available for hunting and sport shooting.

items: Legal battle over federal firearms ban comes to Supreme Court of Canada
Feds extend amnesty period for firearms ban pending Supreme Court ruling

blocks.text: The Federal Court previously ruled in Ottawa's favour, dismissing a request from opponents to strike down the ban for being beyond the scope of the powers of cabinet
Last year, the Federal Court of Appeal rejected an appeal of that decision.

Court of Appeal Chief Justice Yves de Montigny wrote that "surely, the inherent danger that some firearms pose to public safety" and "the increasing demand for measures to address gun violence" are valid considerations in determining whether their use is reasonable for hunting and sporting purposes.
Gun buyback program misses target by nearly half
The appellants argued at the Supreme Court that the two lower courts didn't consider whether the prohibited items were actually used for hunting or sport shooting

"Hunters, sport shooters, collectors and small businesses, individuals who complied with every requirement imposed by Parliament, found themselves overnight in possession of prohibited property, deprived of its lawful use and exposed to the prospect of criminal liability," their submission to the Supreme Court says.
"They are not extremists; they are farmers, veterans, competitive athletes, Indigenous harvesters and neighbours in communities across Canada."
The Supreme Court of Canada has now taken the case under advisement and will issue a decision at a later time — likely not for a few months.
Amnesty period extended

Before the Supreme Court agreed earlier this year to hear the case, the government said the prohibited firearms would have to be disposed of or deactivated by Oct. 30 of this year or owners would face criminal charges.
It then extended the amnesty period until 90 days after the Supreme Court delivers its decision.

Over the past few months, gun owners who declared a prohibited firearm were asked to surrender them if they wanted to be compensated. The federal government has not responded to CBC's request asking how many guns it collected.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Catharine Tunney is a reporter with CBC's Parliament Hill bureau, where she covers national security and the RCMP. She worked previously for CBC in Nova Scotia. You can reach her at catharine.tunney@cbc.ca
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: House Republicans urge DoJ to further investigate ‘key witnesses’ in Epstein case
articles.summary:
Republicans on House panel criticize US government’s investigation into Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell

Republicans on the House oversight committee released a report on Tuesday…

blocks.text: Republicans on the House oversight committee released a report on Tuesday criticizing the federal government’s handling of the investigations into Jeffrey Epstein and his associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, and called on the Department of Justice to interview “key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records”.

“The federal government has failed the survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s horrific crimes for decades,” James Comer, the Republican congressman who chairs the committee, said in a statement.
Comer also urged Congress to pass legislation he introduced that he said would “ensure witnesses and survivors and sexual crimes are not deterred from speaking freely by nondisclosure agreements”.

“We cannot undo the horrific harm inflicted on these women” he said. “But we must ensure that allegations of criminal activity are thoroughly investigated, survivors are protected, and those responsible are held accountable. The failures of the past must not be repeated.”
In a statement, a justice department spokesperson said: “the Chairman’s recommendations have already been addressed.
“The Attorney General has repeatedly said that the Epstein case is not closed and there is no statute of limitations on human trafficking” the spokesperson said.
Shortly after Comer released the report, Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the committee, called the report “misleading” and “partisan”.

“Oversight Republicans have released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein” Garcia said. In his statement, he accused the justice department of continuing to “illegally withhold over 2.5m pages of documents” and said that there has been “no investigation of Ghislaine Maxwell’s transfer, and Attorney General Todd Blanche has yet to testify”.

The majority’s report outlines some of the findings that the oversight committee has come to during their 15-month long investigation into Epstein, including how Epstein cultivated and leveraged relationships with powerful people, and the failures of federal investigators and prosecutors, perhaps most notably the brokering of the controversial non-prosecution agreement and plea deal for Epstein in 2008, which led to his federal case at the time being shelved.
The panel’s investigation has included 19 transcribed interviews and seven depositions.

The report also claims that after the enactment of the Epstein Files Transparency Act last year, the justice department “failed to adequately communicate about document releases and failed to sufficiently protect survivors”.

It adds that “questions remain as to whether the DOJ has released all relevant documents”. Moreover, it states “given the speed with which EFTA records were released, several instances of deficient redaction exposed sensitive information of survivors.”

Among the recommendations, Comer is urging the justice department to further question and investigate Epstein’s longtime assistant, Lesley Groff, who testified before the panel earlier this year. Groff told lawmakers that she had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes while working for him.

Comer also urged the justice department to investigate sexual assault allegations involving two men made by another one of Epstein’s former assistants, Sarah Kellen. Both men have denied any wrongdoing.

The Republican congressman also said the justice department should establish an “appropriate process for Epstein survivors and their representatives to access their personal files and records in unredacted form”, and more.

In a matter of weeks, Democrats will take over the committee in the 120th Congress. Garcia said: “We intend to hold real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump. Our work is just getting started”.

articles.title: Makers of GLP-1 drugs ordered to add warnings about rare eye condition that can lead to blindness
articles.summary: The US Food and Drug Administration says Ozempic, Wegovy, and other weight-loss drugs must have labels about the condition, known as NAION.

blocks.text: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) told makers of popular weight-loss GLP-1 drugs that they must add warning labels about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness.

Manufacturers of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound must warn about nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). The disorder happens when vessels supplying blood to the optic nerves become blocked, depriving the nerves of oxygen.
The condition can cause painless decreased vision in one eye, which can be permanent, the FDA said.
In a statement to the BBC, the American Academy of Ophthalmology said "any added risk appears small, and it has not been established that these medications cause NAION".

"GLP-1 medications offer important benefits for people with diabetes, obesity, and heart disease, so our message to patients is simple," the group said. "Don't stop your medication without talking to your doctor, and if you notice sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, see an ophthalmologist promptly."
There is no known treatment to reverse vision loss caused by NAION. It is the most common cause of acute optic nerve injury in people over 50 years old, according to the academy.

The FDA said it conducted a detailed review of reports of NAION in GLP-1 users as well as a review of other studies and concluded there is an "increased risk of rare NAION events" in people taking the drugs.
In a statement, Novo Nordisk, the manufacturer of Wegovy, one of the most popular weight-loss medications, said the company believes the data "do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship".

"We recognize that NAION can have a profound impact on patients and their families. Patient safety is a top priority for Novo, and we continue to monitor the safety of our medicines," the manufacturer said.

Some research was challenging to review because people taking GLP-1 drugs for obesity and type 2 diabetes may already have risk factors for NAION separate from the drugs, according to the regulator. The FDA said it was not known why those taking GLP-1 drugs may be more at risk for the eye condition.

The drugs already have warning labels for several other conditions including pancreatitis and gallbladder disease. Some of the most common symptoms for semaglutide - a key ingredient in many GLP-1 drugs - include nausea, vomiting and stomach pain.
⁠Last year, a safety arm of the European Medicines Agency, a part of the European Union, said up to 1 in 10,000 people taking semaglutide may be affected by NAION.
In a study published two years ago analysing 17,000 patients, US researchers found those taking semaglutide were four times more likely to be diagnosed with NAION than those not taking the drug.

But one of the authors of the study, Harvard Medical School ophthalmology professor Dr Joseph Rizzo, said the findings were "significant but tentative", and more research was needed on the relationship between the drug and the eye condition in a more diverse population.

articles.title: Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting a devastated front-line city
articles.summary: Slovyansk continues to be bombarded by Russian forces, making it almost uninhabitable with less than 10% of it's pre-war population remaining.

blocks.text: The BBC's Jonathan Beale reported from inside Slovyansk, one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.
The town has become almost uninhabitable and has been under heavy bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.
Members of a Ukrainian drone unit that call themselves Peaky Blinders, named after the cult BBC TV series, have taken on the task of intercepting Russian drones.
Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.

articles.title: Malaysia's disgraced former PM leaves jail for house arrest after embezzling millions
articles.summary: Najib Razak was convicted for his role in the billion-dollar scandal involving the 1MDB sovereign wealth fund.

blocks.text: Najib's mansion in one of the capital's most exclusive neighbourhoods was declared a federal prison ahead of his homecoming on Tuesday.
Critics said his release from jail undermined efforts to fight corruption and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law made no provision for house arrest.
Najib, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2018, denied wrongdoing but was convicted at two separate trials.
In the first trial he was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal.
In September, the King of Malaysia granted him a conditional pardon to see out the remaining two years of his sentence at home.

The transfer to his mansion was to take place on Friday but put on hold after the attorney general sought clarification of the royal decree. On Tuesday the high court ruled the house arrest was effective immediately.
Najib's party paid a $12m fine as part of the terms of the royal pardon allowing him to serve the rest of his term at home.

He was sentenced after being convicted of abuse of power, money laundering and breach of trust over 42 million ringgit ($10m; £7.7m) transferred from SRC International - a former unit of 1MDB - into his private accounts.

Najib is appealing against a 15-year prison sentence, handed down at a second trial in December 2025, in a case involving much larger sums of money. In that case he was convicted of misappropriating nearly 2.3 billion Malaysian ringgit ($569m; £422m) from the nation's sovereign wealth fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
He is due to start serving that sentence after his house arrest ends, which is expected in August 2028.

articles.title: David Walliams, U.K. comedian and author, accused of preying on teenage girls
articles.summary: British comedian and author David Walliams has been accused by multiple women of using his celebrity status to prey on them at a young age, often for sex, according to a three-year investigation by…

image.caption: Comedian David Walliams, pictured here at a movie premier in 2019, has been accused by multiple women of sexual misconduct, including grooming them at a young age. (Henry Nicholls/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

British comedian and author David Walliams has been accused by multiple women of using his celebrity status to prey on them at a young age, often for sex, according to a three-year investigation by the Guardian and ITV News. Walliams has denied the allegations.
Walliams identified as initially-unnamed celebrity who tried to block allegations being published

British comedian and author David Walliams has been accused by multiple women of using his celebrity status to prey on them at a young age, often for sex, according to a three-year investigation by the Guardian and ITV News.

Walliams has also been accused of inappropriate behaviour in the workplace during his time on the show Britain’s Got Talent, where he was a judge for 10 years, and at his former publisher HarperCollins, which has since dropped him.

Walliams has denied the allegations. Earlier this year, his lawyers took a case to the U.K.'s High Court in an effort to stop the Guardian and ITV News from publishing the claims and naming him in their reporting.
A judge rejected his injunction request last week, but protected his identity until late Monday.

That case was dismissed last week, meaning those claims could be shared. Walliams's legal team claimed that if those allegations were made public, he'd take his own life, according to a story by the BBC.
Women accuse Walliams of grooming
While most women say they were over the age of 18 during their interactions with Walliams, two say they were 15 when they first met him.

One woman told the Guardian and ITV News she met Walliams in 2004 at a fan event, when she was 15 and he was 32. He was starring in the hit BBC comedy series Little Britain at the time, and she hoped to one day be a comedy writer.

Matt Lucas, left, and Walliams, right — dressed as their characters Lou Todd and Andy Pipkin — signed copies of their comedy CD in January 2004. It was at such a fan event where one of Walliams' accusers says she first met him. (Steve Finn/Getty Images)

At the event, she says he called her "a very attractive lady" and wouldn't stop staring at her. She gave Walliams some scripts she'd written and her contact information, and after that, she says, he called her at home.
She claims he told her the scripts were very funny, and said they should stay in touch. During the call, she says her age was discussed several times.
As time went on, and communication continued, she says the conversation turned sexual, and Walliams asked for pictures of her naked. At the age of 17, she says her and Walliams had consensual sex.
Walliams told the Guardian and ITV News that he doesn't remember asking for such pictures, and that he believed she was 18 at the time they had sex.

Walliams won a Pride of Britain Award in 2006 as the Most Influential Public Figure, after raising money for the charity campaign Sports Relief by swimming across the English Channel. (Ian Walton/Getty Images)

Another woman also claims to have met Walliams when she was 15, after the two connected on the social network MySpace in 2007. She says they arranged a meet-up when she was in London where they kissed in an alleyway; she said he later touched her sexually at his house and then suggested they connect again when she turned 16.
Walliams denies having sexual contact with the second woman, and says he's never engaged in the grooming of young women.
Other women have also levelled claims that Walliams tried to take advantage of them at a vulnerable age.
Alleged harassment at HarperCollins and Britain's Got Talent

Walliams, who has sold more than 26 million children's books in the U.K. such as Gangsta Granny and Billionaire Boy, was dropped by his publishing company HarperCollins in 2025. The company has since announced it will also no longer publish his back catalogue of books.

According to information obtained by the Guardian and ITV News, that action was taken because of concerns raised over the years, including allegations of an inappropriate sexual relationship with a young female employee.
David Walliams has sold millions of copies of children's books through the publisher HarperCollins, which has since dropped him. (Ben Pruchnie/Getty Images)

Walliams also made a name for himself as one of the judges for Britain's Got Talent from 2012 to 2022. There he was accused of inviting teenage girls to the show as guests, as well as harassing young women who worked on the show.
In November of 2022, Walliams was recorded saying disparaging and sexual comments toward contestants. He has since left the show.
All the while, Walliams and his alleged proclivity to date younger women was the butt of jokes among comedians in the U.K.
'I am not a sexual predator'

Walliams denies any wrongdoing. In a letter to journalists with the Guardian and ITV news who were working on the story, he wrote: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

"I realize I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

Walliams had the opportunity to appeal the High Court's decision allowing the Guardian and ITV News to publish their findings, but Walliams and his legal team didn't file an appeal or request for more time to do so.

articles.title: Judge who sentenced Russell Brand praised for dispelling rape myths
articles.summary:
Criminal Bar Association and campaigners hail Mr Justice Bennathan for delivering remarks with ‘piercing clarity’

The judge who sentenced Russell Brand has been praised for dispelling rape…

blocks.text: The judge who sentenced Russell Brand has been praised for dispelling rape myths with “piercing clarity”.

Mr Justice Bennathan’s sentencing remarks were particularly welcomed given that rape myths had played a part in the trial. He was also lauded for calling out “enablers” who witnessed sexual assaults by the comedian.

Sentencing Brand to 10 and a half years on Monday for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others, Bennathan said: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.”

Andrew Thomas KC, the chair of the Criminal Bar Association, and Kama Melly KC, its vice-chair, said: “We welcome the piercing clarity of the judge’s statement. Myths about rape and sexual assault must play no part in our culture or in our courtrooms. Raping or sexually assaulting someone is a crime, and blame lies entirely with the perpetrator.

“Victims of sexual violence should know that when they go to the prosecution authorities, their evidence will be judged fairly and properly. As the verdicts in Russell Brand’s case show, a properly directed jury will not be put off by a defendant’s appeal to rape myths.”

Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales, said Bennathan’s remarks were “hugely important” at the end of such a high-profile trial. “We’re pleased he emphasised and upheld women’s rights and freedoms, and recognised the profound courage of the women who came forward, and what they endured during the trial, too,” she said.

“This recognition stands in stark contrast to the appalling accusations made by Brand’s defence barrister, who perpetuated myths, misconceptions and conceptions about rape, such as needing to have fought, screamed or reported immediately for it to be considered a credible allegation. Of course this is not the case; there are a range of ways in which people respond to the threat of an imminent sexual assault and all of them are valid.”

blocks.caption: A sketch of Russell Brand listening to a victim impact statement during his sentencing hearing on Monday. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA

blocks.text: Deniz Uğur, the deputy director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, said rape myths should be prohibited. “The judge’s comments are welcome given the significant role that rape myths played in this trial, which in turn have influenced public discussions about the case,” she said. “This will be having a profound effect not only on the women involved in this case, but on survivors exposed to victim-blaming and misconceptions online and in their daily lives.”

On Tuesday, Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, praised Bennathan’s “incredibly powerful” sentencing remarks, contrasting them with the “depressing” nature of the cross-examination of Brand’s victims by his barrister, Ian Winter KC.
after newsletter promotion

The judge also took aim at Brand’s “enablers” who witnessed Brand sexually assault women in front of them at a radio station and TV studio. He said of the former incident: “No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behaviour that only you could get away with. It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offence, and as it turns out you haven’t got away with it.”
Bennathan told Brand the assault at the TV studio showed “your staggering arrogance, and it shows how your entourage indulged your dreadful behaviour”.

Bergman described the comments as “crucial”, adding: “This case and the national response to it is about more than just one man, it is about everyone who laughed along, didn’t speak up and/or looked away, even when it was happening right in front of them. They may not have committed Brand’s crimes, but they contributed to the culture that meant he went on harming other women with impunity for so long.”
Uğur similarly welcomed Bennathan’s remarks, saying it was “critically important to look at the many institutions and individuals that enabled [Brand’s] behaviour”.

In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

articles.title: Woman jailed for posing as man to dupe partner into sex found guilty of similar deception
articles.summary:
Jury finds Blade Silvano, who presented herself as a male army veteran, guilty of six counts of sexual assault

A woman serving a prison sentence for sexual assault after pretending to be a…

blocks.text: A woman serving a prison sentence for sexual assault after pretending to be a man and duping a woman into a physical relationship has been found guilty of tricking another woman into a similar abusive partnership.

In both cases, Blade Silvano, 44, met the women on an online dating site and falsely claimed she was a man who had served in the armed forces before meeting them in person and sexually assaulting them.
Both women said Silvano tricked them into believing she was male and neither had any idea they were being deceived.

Silvano was jailed in 2023 in Cambridge after a jury heard she carried out the deception using a blindfold, sex toy and a “wholly fake persona”. Silvano and her victim even became engaged as a man and woman.

On Tuesday a jury at Caernarfon crown court in north Wales found her guilty of six counts of sexual assault by penetration between November 2022 and the following June after being told she carried out the same sort of deception on another woman.

Using the alias “Hunter”, Silvano began messaging the victim on the Plenty of Fish site before meeting her for sex, always keeping the lights very low and not allowing herself to be touched intimately.

Silvano claimed to be a captain and surgeon in the army and on one occasion claimed “his” condom had broken as they had sex. Silvano assured the alleged victim it was “very unlikely” she would get pregnant and told her: “Trust me, I’m a doctor.”
The jury was told the woman noticed her partner sounded a “little feminine” and began to have doubts about their “odd” sex life.

blocks.caption: Blade Silvano presented herself as a male army veteran on dating site Plenty of Fish. Photograph: CPS/PA

blocks.text: Eventually, the victim received a call from Silvano’s long-term woman partner who said the person she’d known as “Hunter” was female, the court heard.

The victim told police she felt sick when she learned of the deception, saying: “I thought it was some sort of joke.” In court she said: “I believed I was in a relationship with a straight, heterosexual man. I would never go out with a woman.”
Philip Clemo, prosecuting, told the jury Silvano was a gifted con artist and suggested she was inspired by the myth of Zeus turning into a bull.
The Cambridgeshire offences took place in 2016 and 2017. Using the fake name Blade Mendez, Silvano presented herself as a male army veteran throughout a two-year relationship.
She would send the victim photos of herself apparently shaving her face and would pretend to urinate standing up.

Silvano, of Shropshire, would not allow the victim to touch her genitals, claiming to be “body conscious due to injuries sustained in the army”. Silvano and the woman got engaged and she was encouraged to try on wedding dresses and book a registrar.

The victim accidentally uncovered Silvano’s deception after coming across her on Facebook in September 2018 “in a completely different living situation”. Silvano was found guilty of two counts of assault by penetration.
Silvano will be sentenced for the six sexual assaults next month. Judge Jones ordered a pre-sentence report so that the risk she posed could be assessed.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Who is Apollo Quiboloy?
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) reported Tuesday that the US government's request for the extradition of Apollo Quiboloy has been filed before the Makati Regional Trial Court.

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 2:06am
The Department of Justice (DOJ) reported Tuesday that the US government's request for the extradition of Apollo Quiboloy has been filed before the Makati Regional Trial Court.

Quiboloy and several others were indicted by US prosecutors in 2021 for allegedly operating a sex trafficking scheme that threatened victims, some as young as 12, with "eternal damnation" and physical abuse.
The US court issued an arrest warrant for Quiboloy, with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) also seeking his extradition to face charges in the United States.
Who is Quiboloy, and what legal troubles has he faced?
KOJC and political connections
Quiboloy is the founder of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ, The Name Above Every Name (KOJC), a religious organization established in Davao City in 1985.
He is also known by the aliases "Pastor," "ACQ," and "The Appointed Son of God."

Quiboloy broadcast his sermons through various media platforms, including television and radio. According to KOJC, his messages were initially aired through block-time arrangements on different stations before he established Sonshine Media Network International (SMNI).
During the previous administration, Quiboloy was known as a friend and spiritual adviser to former President Rodrigo Duterte.
During Duterte's 2016 presidential campaign, Quiboloy warned in media interviews that any electoral fraud against Duterte would trigger a revolution that he would personally lead.
Duterte was also entrusted with key positions within Quiboloy's religious organization. In March 2024, the former president was appointed administrator of KOJC's properties.
In this capacity, Duterte threatened legal action against police authorities who raided KOJC properties in 2024 as part of operations to serve an arrest warrant against Quiboloy.
Quiboloy also extended his political support to Vice President Sara Duterte, whom he endorsed in the 2022 national elections alongside her running mate, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
In 2019, he also endorsed Imee Marcos in her senatorial bid.
US indictment

In 2021, US prosecutors indicted Quiboloy on sex trafficking charges, alleging that he, along with church officials and two US-based administrators, operated a scheme that coerced girls and young women into sexual relations with him.

"Quiboloy was indicted by a federal grand jury in the United States District Court for the Central District of California, Santa Ana, California, for conspiracy to engage in sex trafficking by force, fraud and coercion and sex trafficking of children; sex trafficking by force, fraud and coercion; conspiracy; and bulk cash smuggling," the FBI said.
The US court issued an arrest warrant for Quiboloy on November 10, 2021.
In 2020, Quiboloy's lawyer, Israelito Torreon, maintained that the religious leader was innocent of the trafficking allegations following a raid on the group's office in the United States.

Earlier that same year, the Davao City Prosecutor's Office dismissed complaints of rape, child abuse, and human trafficking filed against Quiboloy and five other KOJC members, citing insufficient evidence.
In 2022, the FBI released wanted posters for Quiboloy and two other KOJC members, Teresita Tolibas Dandan and Helen Panilag.
By 2024, the Davao-based preacher faced additional legal troubles in the Philippines following a five-month manhunt triggered by a court-issued arrest warrant over child abuse allegations.
He was eventually arrested in September 2024 on charges of violating Republic Act 7610, or the Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation, and Discrimination Act.
He also faces a non-bailable qualified human trafficking charge under Section 4(a) of Republic Act 9208, as amended. – with information from GMA News Research

articles.title: Anti-homosexuality laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
articles.summary: The ruling brings to an end an 11-year legal battle by dual-citizen Jason Jones.

blocks.text: A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.

London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."
The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."
Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.
It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.
Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.
Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.

The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.

Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.
The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.
Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".
Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.
"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."
Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."
