articles.title: US federal authorities could have prevented Epstein crimes, report finds
articles.summary: The report by a Republican-led congressional committee follows a 15-month investigation into the handling of the late disgraced financier's case.

blocks.text: Regarding Epstein's death in a New York prison, investigators concluded this was a result of "a series of institutional failures at the facility," which included staffing shortages, overworked employees, poor recordkeeping, and lax security practices.
Testimony the panel solicited was "unable to definitively dispel certain theories" surrounding Epstein's death, the report states, including accounting for a lapse in surveillance footage.
It found the justice department (DoJ) failed to communicate about document releases and that deficient redactions exposed survivors' sensitive personal information.
Earlier this year, the DoJ had to remove thousands of documents related to Epstein from its website after victims said their identities had been compromised.

The report also alleges that financial institutions like American Express enabled human trafficking and immigration fraud, by allowing Epstein to use decoy flights and dummy itineraries to transport foreign workers across borders. The BBC has contacted American Express for comment.
The investigative panel recommended that Congress should pass legislation to prevent the weaponisation of non-disclosure agreements, which they said Epstein used to silence survivors.
"Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims," said James Comer, the Republican chairman of the committee.
He called upon the DoJ to "interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records.
The report accuses Democrats of being "obsessed" with trying to implicate US President Donald Trump and that an "unfounded witch hunt continued without regard for the interests of survivors".

Trump has previously said he was friendly with Epstein before they fell out in 2004. The president's name has appeared thousands of times in the Epstein files but there is no suggestion that appearing in the documents implies any wrongdoing.
The committee's review of documents did not identify any that would implicate Trump, the report concluded.

In a statement, Rep Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, alleged his Republican colleagues "released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein".
Garcia accused the justice department of withholding "over 2.5 million pages of documents".

"We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation," said Garcia, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control of Congress in January following the recent midterm elections.

articles.title: Activist wins 10-year fight against homophobic Trinidad and Tobago laws
articles.summary:
Jason Jones welcomes decision by privy council in London to overturn 2025 ruling that outlawed anal sex

A gay man has won a historic 10-year battle against Trinidad and Tobago’s homophobic…
articles.byline: Natricia Duncan, Joshua Surtees and Kejan Haynes

blocks.text: A gay man has won a historic 10-year battle against Trinidad and Tobago’s homophobic laws with a landmark UK appeals court ruling that could help overturn similar anti-gay laws in other Caribbean countries.

The privy council, based in London, overturned a 2025 decision by Trinidad and Tobago’s court of appeal that recriminalised consensual anal sex, seven years after the Trinidadian activist Jason Jones secured a high court judgment declaring the country’s colonial-era “buggery” laws unconstitutional.
In explaining its ruling on Tuesday, the court said: “The ability to form a deep connection with another person through an intimate and loving relationship is a vital interest for all human beings.”
“This judgment will have a domino effect across every country that has the privy council as its supreme court. It will change many millions of people’s lives,” Jones said in a statement.
“I’m looking forward to going home, switching off everything and living with this moment for a while.”
His lawyers hailed Tuesday’s unanimous judgment as a “phenomenal victory”.
“The judgment recognises the human reality at the heart of the case,” the statement from Freedom Law Chambers said.

“It expressly recognised that a loving relationship between two men engages the constitutional protection of family life. For LGBTQ+ people who have lived with stigma, fear and the threat of criminal punishment, that recognition has profound personal significance.”

The privy council is the final court of appeal for Trinidad and Tobago and several other Commonwealth countries, giving the ruling potentially far-reaching significance for other Caribbean jurisdictions where similar laws remain in force.

Jones has been fighting the “buggery law”, whose origins date to British colonial rule, for a decade. In a historic 2018 victory, high court judge Devindra Rampersad ruled that the provisions criminalising consensual anal sex were unconstitutional. But the government appealed, and in 2025 the court of appeal overturned that decision.

Tuesday’s privy council decision restores Jones’s victory, with all five judges finding that sections 13 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act 1986 must be interpreted consistently with the constitution so that they do not criminalise private, consensual sexual relations between adults of the same sex.

It marks the latest significant advance for LGBTQ+ rights in the Caribbean, after a landmark ruling in St Lucia last year, when the Eastern Caribbean supreme court struck down colonial-era laws criminalising consensual gay sex.

Asked whether this would make Jones, who has lived in London for several decades, feel comfortable living in Trinidad again, he said no. “The thing about liberation movements is every time you move the needle forward, you get the pushback. I got a lot of pushback from the queer community [in Trinidad] saying: ‘Don’t stir the pot.’ But you have to. I’m not afraid of pushback.”

articles.title: Victims of Nazi war in Poland call on Germany for support
articles.summary: More than 80 years after the end of World War II, Polish victims of the Nazi regime are still waiting for a "humanitarian gesture" from Germany. The 2027 draft budget hasn't left them much hope for…

image.caption: The former Nazi regime forced thousands of Polish people to work in Germany under inhumane conditions during World War IIImage: picture alliance

blocks.text: "We can no longer wait," declared Polish victims' organizations in a dramatic appeal to German civil society, published on November 5 on the website of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation.

"Around 50,000 survivors of Nazi persecution during the German occupation still live in Poland today. They include former concentration camp and prison inmates, people deported to Germany for forced labor and those subjected to other forms of Nazi repression," wrote the signatories of the appeal.

The open letter pointed out that many of the survivors are over 90 years old, struggling with illness and rising costs, and in need of help in their daily lives. "For many, any further delay in deciding to provide assistance means that help will come too late," said the appeal, which was distributed in German, Polish and English.

blocks.caption: Unresolved issues of reparations have strained relations between Germany and Poland for decadesImage: AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: While Germany has recognized its moral responsibility toward the remaining survivors of Nazi persecution, the signatories pointed out that a corresponding decision on possible reparations by the German federal government has yet to be made.

"Today, we appeal primarily to German civil society to provide humanitarian support to survivors of Nazi persecution living in Poland," they wrote, addressing businesses, foundations, associations and private citizens. "Every donation matters."
Reparations offered to date seen as insufficient
The unresolved issue of war reparations has clouded German-Polish relations for decades.

Following the 1989 democratic transition in Central and Eastern Europe and the reunification of Germany, the federal government provided 500 million deutschmarks to Holocaust victims in Poland. More than 1 million people received support through these funds. Former forced laborers also received payments from the EVZ Foundation, which works to preserve the memory of the victims of National Socialist persecution.

However, given the scale of German crimes during World War II, the reparations provided to date have been considered as insufficient by large parts of Polish society. German occupation policy in Poland was characterized by systematic crimes against the Polish population. An estimated 6 million Polish citizens were killed during the war, including about 3 million Polish Jews.
At 100, Auschwitz survivor recalls life during the Holocaust

As part of the "General Plan East," a large portion of the population was to be displaced, enslaved or murdered. As early as 1939, the "Intelligenzaktion" specifically targeted the Polish elites, including teachers, clergy, civil servants and intellectuals. In addition, approximately 2.5 million Poles were deported to the German Reich for forced labor and made to work there under inhumane conditions.

When it came to power in 2015, Poland's right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) made the issue of war reparations a central focus of Warsaw's policy toward Berlin. The PiS government estimated Poland's war losses at 6.2 trillion zloty (approx. €1.3 trillion/$1.58 trillion) and officially demanded this sum from Berlin in October 2022.
Tusk rejects €200 million as insufficient

The center-left government led by Donald Tusk has distanced itself from these demands since Tusk's election victory in December 2023. However, the government has also made no secret of the fact that Poland is expecting a "creative solution" from its German partner, according to Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski.

blocks.caption: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk (front) has made no secret of the fact that he's waiting for a 'creative solution' from Germany Image: Kacper Pempel/REUTERS

blocks.text: Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz had offered €200 million ($224 million) prior to his visit to Poland in the summer of 2024, an offer rejected by Tusk as insufficient. The talks held since then between Berlin and Warsaw have failed to produce a solution.

In a final declaration following the German-Polish government consultations in December 2025, the German government promised to "analyze possibilities for additional support for Polish victims of Nazi aggression and the German occupation of Poland."

"Currently, there is no decision regarding a humanitarian gesture and the draft budget reflects this status," Josef Hinterseher, deputy spokesperson for Germany's Federal Foreign Office, told reporters on September 23.
Germany's Greens still hope for 'humanitarian gesture'
Germany's opposition Greens party has not given up hope of a turnaround in its efforts to secure a "humanitarian gesture."

"Our parliamentary group submitted a request to the budget committee to secure funding for this 'humanitarian gesture.' Unfortunately, the request was rejected," Franziska Brantner, co-chair of the Greens, told DW on Thursday in Warsaw.

blocks.caption: Green co-leader Franziska Brantner hasn't given up hope that Germany will still change its stance on Polish reparationsImage: Michaela Küfner/DW

blocks.text: "Hope dies last, so we will do everything in our power to ensure that the coalition makes this change after all," she emphasized. Brantner sees the budget committee's "final review session," which will take place this week, as a last chance.

The issue of reparations still plays an important role in Polish society, even more than 80 years after the end of the war. There is hardly a family that did not suffer during the war. In the latest German-Polish Barometer — a representative survey that has been conducted for 25 years — 53% of respondents stated that the suffering of the Polish people is not sufficiently acknowledged in Germany. Only 18% believed that the Germans have done enough.
German private donors support the victims' fund

Jakub Deka, chairman of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation, believes the appeal by the victims' associations could now mobilize Germany's civil society. Following an initial appeal in May directed at the German federal government, several hundred Germans responded with donations ranging from €50 to several hundred euros.

To date, a total of more than €35,000 ($39,000) has been deposited into the foundation's account. Several people in need have already received one-time assistance from this fund. "It's a drop in the bucket, but every little bit helps," Deka told DW.

The foundation's chairman quotes Jerzy Tarasiewicz — who led the victims' association in the Polish city of Gdansk for many years — as a cautionary reminder. In January, Tarasiewicz was quoted in an interview with the daily newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza as saying: "They [the Germans] are waiting for us to die."
Tarasiewicz, who was born in 1942 on a German farm where his parents were performing forced labor, died in late September at the age of 84 without being able to witness this "humanitarian gesture."
"It is a painful reminder that the victims cannot wait any longer," said Deka.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Ottawa consulting on future of Arctic offshore oil and gas drilling ban, Carney says
articles.summary: The federal government says it is building up the "capacity" for northern communities to consult on the future of Canada's moratorium on oil and gas drilling in the Arctic.

image.caption: The Beaufort Sea off the coast of Alaska is seen in 2017. (David Goldman/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics
The federal government says it is building up the "capacity" for northern communities to consult on the future of Canada's moratorium on oil and gas drilling in the Arctic.
Funding plans were buried in Budget 2026 document

Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed the federal government is working with northern governments and the Inuvialuit, the Inuit whose land claim includes much of the waters in the Beaufort Sea, on whether to keep the moratorium.

Other news outlets, including the National Observer, have reported on the government's plans, which were buried in its Budget 2026 document. The federal budget contains $11 million over four years for Arctic offshore oil and gas governance.
Northern premiers, including Nunavut's, have said they are interested in lifting the drilling ban.
Although talks are happening with territorial governments and the Inuvialuit, Carney was quick to say the ban on drilling remains in place.
Budget's offshore gas funding 'absolutely not' a decision to lift Arctic drilling moratorium, Carney says

"It is absolutely not in any way, shape or form a decision about lifting the moratorium. It is a respectful engagement," Carney said. "It's respecting [Indigenous] self-government. But it's also, rest assured, respecting the environment."
Carney said the $11 million would be used for capacity funding across a wide northern area that's co-managed by the Inuvialuit and the territorial and federal governments.
In 2016, Trudeau government alongside U.S. President Barack Obama closed the door to future offshore oil and gas activity in both Canadian and American Arctic waters. Canada declared a five-year ban.
Offshore drilling in deep Arctic waters poses unique challenges. Oil and gas company Chevron put their plans on hold "indefinitely" in 2014 citing "the level of economic uncertainty in the industry."

The company's plans faced scrutiny and questions about whether it could contain a catastrophic blowout, the kind seen in the Gulf of Mexico in 2010. The explosion on the BP-leased Deepwater Horizon resulted in the largest marine oil spill in history.
The Arctic's narrow ice season constrains the ability to bring in equipment to drill a relief well that could stop an oil spill.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.title: Britain willing to discuss paying into EU to join electricity market, says minister
articles.summary:
Hamish Falconer says UK has ‘not accepted principle’ of linking electricity trade to ‘cohesion fund’ but two sides will discuss issue

Britain is willing to discuss paying towards…

blocks.text: Britain is willing to discuss paying towards infrastructure schemes in poorer parts of the EU in return for access to the European electricity market, according to the minister in charge of renegotiating the bilateral relationship.

Hamish Falconer, the cabinet minister in charge of EU talks, told the Guardian he was sure the two sides would discuss the issue after this month’s summit, as ministers look to deepen ties with the union over the next few years.

Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has said he wants a much closer relationship with the EU in the future, even raising the possibility of rejoining as a full member. But while senior figures in Brussels have said they are keen to discuss such an idea, they also want to see the UK begin to start paying for access to the European schemes it says it wants.
This weekend five European leaders welcomed the UK’s desire to join the European electricity market, but said Britain would have to pay into a so-called “cohesion fund” in order to do so.
While UK officials say they do not accept the link between the electricity reforms and cohesion fund, the minister admitted the UK would enter into talks about additional contributions.

“We have not accepted that principle,” Falconer said. “I understand that that’s what the European Union have asked for, but the UK government hasn’t accepted. Again, this is something no doubt we will discuss.”

blocks.caption: Falconer outside 10 Downing Street in September. Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty Images

blocks.text: Falconer has said he hopes next week’s keenly anticipated EU-UK summit “will go some real distance in undoing some of the harm that Brexit has done”. Negotiators hope to sign deals on food and drink, carbon emissions and youth mobility.

Any move to bring Britain into the EU electricity market, however, is likely to prove controversial. The EU cohesion fund promotes economic development in poorer regions in the bloc and UK officials will be cautious about any deal in which British taxpayers’ money could be spent on infrastructure projects in central and eastern Europe.

Falconer was, however, clear that the UK would be keen to join a future EU defence fund. Last year, negotiations on Britain’s entry into the EU’s €150bn (£125bn) defence fund collapsed after a dispute over the UK’s contribution.
The UK had been seeking to join the first round of the EU’s Security Action for Europe (Safe) fund, a low-interest loan scheme that is part of the EU’s push to grow defence spending by €800bn.

EU officials suggested an entry fee of up to €6bn, significantly higher than the administrative fee the government had anticipated, and talks collapsed. “I think it’s a real shame that the UK was not part of that scheme,” Falconer said on Monday.

“The terms on which we were asked to join were clearly not terms that we could agree and I think that’s a shame – and I think lots of our friends in the EU think it was a shame … so I hope there is an opportunity for a Safe2 and one in which the UK could join on reasonable terms.”

Falconer also said he hoped negotiators would agree a youth mobility scheme ready for the 20 November summit, though there have been crucial sticking points over demands for home tuition fees for EU students at UK universities.

The Guardian reported last week that the UK was prepared to spend up to £450m a year to give EU students discounted university tuition fees, if Brussels allowed Britain access to the Made in Europe industrial programme.

“Obviously I understand that there are a number of member states who would like to see it made easier for EU students to come to the UK and have lower fees than they currently pay if they want to go to British universities,” Falconer said on Monday.

“But that is outside of the common understanding so it will require a different set of arrangements than were envisaged when these negotiations started. Clearly it’s something that on the EU side there’s real interest, so we are engaging in that discussion but I can’t comment in detail on the negotiations.”

Falconer was firmly positive about the UK’s return next year to the Erasmus+ student exchange scheme, which the UK left under Boris Johnson’s Brexit deal in 2020, and will be open not just to universities but also to schools and colleges.

“I hope around the start of the summit we will be opening applications for British young people to put themselves right in the heart of Europe,” he said, rejecting Nigel Farage’s criticisms of Erasmus and the youth mobility scheme as opening the door to uncontrolled immigration.

“People understand that it is a good thing for our young people to be able to travel widely in Europe, to be able to study, to have the kind of exchanges that make such a big difference to people’s lives.
“I think honestly Nigel Farage is being a big old grinch about this. This is in the interests of our young people and he should give his head a bit of a wobble, I think.”

articles.title: Russian naval aggression prompts new defensive initiative with ‘beer-drinking nations’
articles.summary:
New alliance with the Netherlands and Baltic and Nordic countries comes in response to 41% increase in Russian naval activity around UK

Russian naval activity around the UK has increased by…

blocks.text: Russian naval activity around the UK has increased by 41% in the first nine months of the year, a British defence minister said, as the Royal Navy announced plans to step up a 10-country maritime defensive effort in response.

Luke Pollard, minister for defence readiness, described the figure as “a huge increase”, justifying a new drone and warship initiative from “the alliance of beer-drinking nations” – the UK, the Netherlands and the Baltic and Nordic countries.

The plan is for sea drones from the UK and other countries to be able to work interchangeably with warships from countries across the Northern Navies Initiative at a time when the number of British frigates is falling.

“The model that we want is where British autonomy [drones] can be teamed with a British warship or a Danish warship or a Norwegian warship and can hand that autonomy off to an allied nation’s warship,” Pollard said.

A future Royal Navy would combine warships and drones “because that would increase our lethality”, Pollard said, sidestepping a debate about the number of UK frigates – which could drop from 12 in 2021 to three by 2030.

Last month, the cross-party defence select committee warned that the navy risked failing to deter Russian aggression in the seas around the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability of warships and submarines.

Pollard blamed the Conservatives for capacity shortfalls, accusing them of cutting budgets and delaying investment when they were in government. “Now, because of the decisions taken 10, 15 years ago, we have fewer ships and fewer submarines than I would like available,” the minister said.

An extra £10bn a year allocated to defence in 2030 by chancellor John Healey in October’s budget means that the UK could “send a clear demand signal to industry”, the minister said, to help tackle the Russian threat.

However, since the budget announcement, there have been no major defence spending announcements, with the UK sticking to the defence investment plan which was announced in June and fully funded in the budget. That included a £1.5bn investment in sea drones over four years.

Russian spy ships, such as the Yantar, have been sailing near UK waters this year trying to obtain “an increased picture of our critical national infrastructure”, Pollard said, as well as “mapping our undersea cables”.

Its frigates have also been active in the North Sea and the Channel throughout 2026, often escorting oil tankers and other trade vessels, and at one point firing shots near a pleasure yacht south of the Isle of Wight in June.

Oil tankers linked to Russia remained active, though were now often “sailing around the UK” to avoid coming through the Channel, Pollard said, after the seizure of one Russia-linked tanker, the Smyrtos, in the same month as the shooting incident.

The minister insisted that, if necessary, the Royal Navy was “ready to fight tonight”, even though it took three weeks for the UK to send a destroyer to Cyprus in the spring after the UK base at Akrotiri was struck by a drone fired by an Iranian proxy.

Russia’s northern fleet, based in the Barents Sea, retains “a really formidable undersea presence”, Pollard said, adding that Moscow had continued to invest in it throughout the Ukraine war as a means of threatening the UK.

The minister was speaking at the navy’s International Sea Power conference held on the Prince of Wales aircraft carrier in Oslo. Sailing the warship to Norway was “a really important deterrent signal that we stand ready to defend every single inch of Nato territory”, he said.

A further £90m will be spent on underwater drones and sensors to monitor the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap for Russian submarine activity, considered to be a strategic choke point in what the navy describes as the “high north”.
Ukraine has used cheap sea drones to destroy around a third of Russia’s Black Sea fleet, forcing it to relocate from Sevastopol in occupied Crimea to Novorossiysk, on the eastern Black Sea.

The former head of the country’s military, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, now Ukraine’s ambassador to the UK, said the increasingly complex use of sea drones meant that “it is likely that the world’s navies are on the verge of the most radical transformation since the rise of torpedo technology”.

articles.title: 'The editor's here!': CBC journalist stars in viral video with American stand-up Josh Johnson
articles.summary: A CBC News copy editor turned into one half of an unexpected comedy duo in a video posted to social media Tuesday. American comedian Josh Johnson brought Jon Azpiri to the stage to talk cats,…

image.caption: Comedian Josh Johnson, left, and CBC News copy editor and reporter Jon Azpiri, right, talk onstage in Vancouver at the Vogue Theatre on Oct. 23. (Josh Johnson/Facebook)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

A CBC News copy editor turned into one half of an unexpected comedy duo in a video posted to social media Tuesday. American comedian Josh Johnson brought Jon Azpiri to the stage to talk cats, disappearing islands and journalism.
Copy editor Jon Azpiri called onstage to share the ins and outs of CBC's Journalistic Standards and Practices
A CBC News copy editor turned into one half of an unexpected comedy duo in a video posted to social media Tuesday.

American comedian Josh Johnson, a stand-up and occasional host of The Daily Show, was cracking jokes about CBC's coverage of a bodega cat getting evicted due to health concerns, during his show at the Vogue Theatre in Vancouver last month.
"I want so badly to meet the editor," Johnson quipped.
A voice from the audience shouted out: "He's here!"
A befuddled Johnson replied: "The cat's here?"
Nope.
"The editor's here!" shouted the crowd.
Enter Jon Azpiri.

Wearing a dark grey hoodie, coincidentally mirroring Johnson's signature light grey hoodie, Azpiri walked onstage for a 10-minute back-and-forth filled with jokes about cats, disappearing islands and journalism.

items: An island mysteriously appeared — then disappeared — on B.C.'s largest reservoir

blocks.text: Johnson started to ask Azpiri about the bodega cat situation before Azpiri interrupted.
"We do a lot of stories about cats. So I need to know the specific cat."
Azpiri, a copy editor and reporter, answered Johnson's various questions about how a newsroom chooses what to cover.
"We're a public broadcaster," Azpiri said. "So we have a thing called Journalistic Standards and Practices."
"There's really no need to brag," Johnson replied.

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: As of 9:30 a.m. PT, Johnson's video shared on Instagram has more than 1.2 million views.
Johnson ended the exchange, and the two shook hands.
As Azpiri left, he reminded Johnson the province was set to have an election the next day.
"That's a real editor right there, too," Johnson said. "Even as he's leaving, [he's like] 'We do have an election tomorrow.'"
CBC News has reached out to Johnson.

articles.title: Inside devastated front-line city that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
articles.summary: The BBC gains rare access to a specialist drone unit defending the eastern city of Slovyansk from heavy Russian fire.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Moose Campbell
Ukraine's Peaky Blinders drone unit wear flat caps, a nod to the cult TV series from which they take their name
ByJonathan Beale
Defence correspondentReporting fromSlovyansk, eastern Ukraine
The dangers in Slovyansk are clear from the start.
"If I say run, you run," Tetiana tells us. She and her colleague Yasha are escorting us into a city now under constant bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.
It is raining and cloudy as we enter the city, and our military escorts call this "good" weather, meaning it is bad for drones.
But the threat is still there, and Yasha keeps his eyes peeled on the skies, while 21-year-old Tetiana scours her phone for the latest military intelligence on likely threats from the air.
They are members of a drone unit who call themselves Peaky Blinders and their distinctive emblem is a flat cap of the type made popular by the cult BBC TV series, although theirs are camouflaged.
Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.
Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.
Ukrainians worry that doing so would make it much easier for Russia to advance further west, including to the capital Kyiv.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Very little of the city has been left unscathed by months of heavy bombardment

blocks.text: Very little of the city has been left unscathed by months of heavy bombardment

Once inside the city, we leave our vehicles hidden under the cover of trees and venture out on foot. Yasha carries a shotgun – a last resort to shoot down Russian drones. In halting English, Tetiana tells us walking is safer than travelling by car.
Abandoned vehicles litter the streets – recently destroyed by remotely operated Russian first-person view drones. The anti-drone netting that covers the roads is no guarantee of safety.
Tetiana shows us a video on her phone taken a few days earlier.

You can hear several drones buzzing above her, and then the cacophony of small arms fire as Ukrainian forces try to shoot them down. Tetiana admits it can be scary but explains how she felt compelled to help her country, abandoning her dreams of becoming an opera singer.
Slovyansk is now a husk of its former self. Very few buildings have been left unscathed, with many reduced to rubble.

Tetiana shows us a school recently destroyed by Russian glide bombs. Across the road there is a gaping hole in an abandoned residential block. Broken glass litters the pavement. The few shops still functioning are boarded up – making it hard to distinguish what is still open. Most have closed.

Tetiana says the Russians are doing everything they can to intimidate people and drive them out of the city. That, she says, "is their strategy – to make people leave in chaos, gathering up their last belongings and fleeing amid enormous fear and suffering. They want people to have nowhere left to live".

It is a familiar pattern already seen in other Ukrainian towns and cities in the Donbas – like Pokrovsk and Bakhmut. These are now ghost towns reduced to rubble, but eventually falling into Russian hands.

blocks.caption: Map showing the four fortress cities in Ukraine's Donbas - with Russia's military advance in Ukraine shown in red

blocks.text: Russia has already taken nearly 90% of the Donbas – made up of the regions of Luhansk and Donetsk - but its advances this year have all but stalled in the face of strong Ukrainian resistance.
The White House is sounding positive about the revived talks in Abu Dhabi, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's refusal to cede the territory.

October was the deadliest month for Russian troops since the start of its full-scale invasion – with more than 54,000 killed or injured, according to Ukraine's general staff. Despite this, Russian forces are still making life in the Fortress Belt cities almost impossible.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Iryna, who works in one of the city's last remaining cafes, is one of the few residents who decided to stay

blocks.text: Iryna, who works in one of the city's last remaining cafes, is one of the few residents who decided to stay
Before the war, Slovyansk was a city of more than 200,000 people. Less than 10% of those remain and the population diminishes by the day.

But amid the wail of near constant air raid warnings, there are still signs of people clinging on to life here. Iryna works in one of the city's last remaining coffee shops. Slovyansk is where she was born.
"I'm forced to walk around crying," she tells me. "How can they do this?"
Life, she says, has become incredibly difficult. She has already lost her house. But despite her tears, there is still defiance: "I won't leave Slovyansk. This is my home."
Inga, 53, was also born and raised here and continues to work in the city despite the danger.
"It's stressful. Honestly, I don't even know what to say," she says, but she is staying because of what she calls the "fear of the unknown".
"I simply have nowhere to go, and I don't have the money to leave or support myself afterwards." Nor, she says, is there anywhere else in Ukraine she would consider truly safe.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Commander Oleksandr says neither side is able to advance because of the large number of drones in use

blocks.text: Commander Oleksandr says neither side is able to advance because of the large number of drones in use
We first met the drone unit two years ago fighting in the Kharkiv region, in north-eastern Ukraine.
Just four of the original team remain - the rest have moved to other units, or they have been wounded or killed.
Among the dead was the brother of the man in charge of the unit, Oleksandr, who now describes his unit as his family.
He jokes it is just like the Peaky Blinders TV show – "but without the crime and the drugs". Back at their base they share a meal every evening.

Oleksandr reads out a prayer of thanks for surviving another day – he says it strengthens their spirits. The meal is accompanied by classical music played on a speaker. It helps drown out the noise of the explosions nearby.
"I feel this is the most difficult situation we've ever faced," says Oleksandr, who underlines the importance of holding the line.

"We must be here to inflict maximum damage on the enemy. We're fighting here because this is where the most intense phase of the war is taking place. Russia's claim that they will reach the borders of the Donbas, seize it, and then the war will end is absolutely false," he insists.

The remaining fortress belt cities provide Ukraine with a strong defensive line and are a major obstacle to any Russian advance. The saturation of drones in the area is also now making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance here.
Peace talks may have resumed, but Oleksandr notes they have not led to anything so far.
"I really want this war to end," he says, "but do I believe these negotiations will succeed? No, I don't really believe they will".

blocks.caption: Image caption, The streets are largely empty, with increasing numbers of residents evacuated as drone attacks intensify

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
The streets are largely empty, with increasing numbers of residents evacuated as drone attacks intensify
The next morning we are not the only ones making an exit. A dozen civilians have arrived at an evacuation point in the centre to be escorted out.
They hold all the belongings they can carry and are taken into a bunker for their safety. Outside there is another heavy blast of small arms fire, signalling more drones are nearby.

Alina Shyrko, herself a resident of Slovyansk, is co-ordinating the move of civilians out of the city and says the situation has deteriorated rapidly over the past few months. Families with children have already been ordered to leave.
"Everyone is thinking about leaving," she says, "I'm thinking about it too."
Ukraine still holds Slovyansk but its lifeblood, its people, are ebbing away.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 41: Contempt warning, salary differential, witness's accounting firm ties
articles.summary: Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis Escudero opened the 41st day of the impeachment trial by warning witnesses against lying or mocking the court, saying they could be held in contempt.

blocks.text: Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis Escudero opened the 41st day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte by warning witnesses against lying or mocking the court, saying they could be held in contempt.

This came a day after defense witness and Davao City Assessor James Adalin was seen smiling during his testimony and telling private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. that the latter's question about his trip to China was irrelevant.

Engineer John Kenneth Enumerables, assessor of the Island Garden City of Samal, then testified that he was unsure whether the property in Samal acquired by Duterte's husband, Manases Carpio, in 2013 was the same property declared in their joint Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) from 2015 onward.
Enumerables said he could not confirm this because the SALN did not indicate the property's Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT).

Senator-judges also reminded him to clarify the records concerning the property's location, as land titles in the area indicate Barangay Matanos while its tax declaration and other documents identify it as Barangay San Isidro.
Before the noon break, the defense and prosecution panels raised concerns over possible violations of the sub judice rule.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison said Tolosa's statements did not constitute fair commentary, while Tolosa argued that statements made by the Vice President against the prosecution and the impeachment court not only violated the sub judice rule but also unfairly attacked the integrity of the impeachment proceedings.

Davao City Accountant Vingelin Bajan testified that Duterte received P64,194.72 from the Davao City government in January 2023 as payment for salary differentials dating back to her previous terms as city mayor.
Bajan confirmed a summary of payroll records showing that Duterte was entitled to P64,194.72 in salary differentials for 2020 and 2021, when she was still Davao City mayor.
The payout was made only in January 2023 because the supporting documents were completed only at that time, Bahan said.

Bajan, however, was unable to immediately confirm her previous ties to an accounting firm associated with businesses linked to the Vice President and her husband, even after being confronted with official documents bearing her signature.

Private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia said Bajan was formerly a partner at Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co., CPAs, citing Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) records, including the firm's 2003 Articles of Partnership, which bore her signature as a partner.
Divinagracia asked Bajan to confirm her signature in the SEC records, but the witness initially could not provide an answer.

Bajan repeatedly said she could not recall details about her former employment but later admitted that she had indeed been a partner at the firm. She said she left in 2015 for personal reasons after further questioning from Divinagracia and the senator-judges.
The atmosphere turned lighter when Divinagracia asked Bajan about her December 2025 trip to China. The witness said it was a reward for herself and her friends after putting in long hours at work.

The hearing, however, turned serious again when Divinagracia pointed out that the P64,194.72 salary differential Duterte received from the Davao City government in 2023 was not reflected in the Vice President's income tax return for the following year.
Divinagracia cited Duterte's 2024 annual income tax return, which did not indicate any compensation received from either the Davao City government or the Office of the Vice President (OVP).
Bajan said she could not confirm the figures reflected in the Vice President's income tax return.

Meanwhile, defense spokesperson and lawyer Michael Poa said the defense was surprised to learn about Bajan's links to the accounting firm associated with businesses linked to the Vice President and her husband.
Poa also maintained that the defense did not prepare its witnesses for their testimonies.

In a press conference after the hearing, Tolosa said the prosecution would ask the impeachment court to sanction Duterte and her spokesperson, lawyer Paolo Panelo, over statements that allegedly violated the sub judice rule, including remarks questioning the integrity of the court.

“We've heard that from the Vice President time and again, as well as her spokesperson attacking their integrity, attacking their motives, saying the impeachment proceedings have been marred by bending the law, saying that senators are manipulating the proceedings, and that the budget is being used to control the senators. These [statements] touched not just the merits of the case but also attack the integrity of the court,” Tolosa said.
Ahead of the 41st day of the impeachment trial, Escudero expressed hope that the proceedings would be completed within the year.

Escudero, however, clarified that the impeachment court was not following a fixed timeline and that he could not say exactly when the trial would end, as this would depend on the evidence presented by the defense and the flow of the hearings.

The defense is presenting its evidence against Article 2 of the impeachment complaint, which accuses the Vice President of betrayal of public trust and culpable violation of the Constitution over alleged unexplained wealth amounting to P817 million to P1.5 billion, stemming from the alleged non-declaration of assets and failure to divest from businesses despite a constitutional prohibition. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Twelve dead after motorway pile-ups in Bulgaria fog
articles.summary: About 50 other people were injured in the pile-ups along a section of the Trakia motorway, officials have said.

blocks.text: Burnt out and crushed vehicles were strew across the motorway in the aftermath of the crash
Twelve people have been killed after dozens of cars and lorries were involved in two pile-ups on the Trakia motorway in south-eastern Bulgaria, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said.
Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 11 people died at the scene on Tuesday, near the town of Zimnitsa, while another person later died in hospital. About 50 others were taken to hospital with injuries.
Sliven regional governor Mihail Kasherov told journalists that more than 70 vehicles were involved in the incident, Bulgarian state news agency BTA reported.
Officials have said dense fog reduced visibility and was the likely cause of the first crash, which occurred on the eastbound carriageway.
Radev declared Wednesday a day of national mourning following the incident.

blocks.caption: BBC map of Bulgaria showing the A1 motorway, known as the Trakia Highway, as a red line running east-west across the middle of the country, from Sofia in the west, passing north of Plovdiv, and then all the way to Burgas on the Black Sea coast in the east. A black dot near the town of Zimnitsa, a…

blocks.text: The second crash, on the Sofia-bound carriageway, was likely also caused by the fog, with drivers also distracted by the first crash, BTA reported an official as saying.
The Trakia motorway runs from west-to-east of Bulgaria, and connects the capital Sofia to the Black Sea coast.

Road administration director Galin Kostov added that speeds were unsuitable for the conditions, which included wet road surfaces, and the motorway would remain closed until it had been cleared, BTA reported.
Yambol regional governor Georgi Chalakov said reports first came in at 07:10 local time (05:10 GMT), with the injured taken by ambulance to hospitals in the Yambol, Sliven and Burgas regions.
Chalakov told BTA rescue teams had to remove sections of the crash barrier to reach people. He added that the fog meant that helicopters could not be used in the evacuation efforts.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A drone captured the scene from above, just visible through the dense fog

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
A drone captured the scene from above, just visible through the dense fog
One witness who helped rescue a man from a burning vehicle blamed "very thick fog" for the pile-up.
"I got out of the car, I ran forward and pulled that man out," the witness told Reuters news agency.
Another told Reuters that "many, many people died".
"As for me, there were four cars behind me - trucks - and I don't know how I got out or what happened, but in the end, thank God I'm still alive," that witness said.
Radev - who had been hosting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen - cut short a news conference after learning of the incident and visited the scene.

articles.title: Gibo warns Pinoys of being brainwashed while in China
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. cautioned Filipinos against being “brainwashed” during their trips or vacations in China.

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. cautioned Filipinos against being “brainwashed” during their trips or vacations in China.
He said there is nothing wrong with visiting China, but he warned of being fed wrong information or misled to believe false narratives.
“Yes, go to China,” Teodoro said in a Facebook post yesterday, apparently reacting to reports on a surge of visa applications by Filipinos wanting to visit China.

“Enjoy the beautiful culture but do not, do not be brainwashed,” said the DND chief, who has been banned from entering Chinese territory along with his family because of his unwavering stand against China’s illegal, coercive, aggressive and deceptive activities in the West Philippine Sea (WPS).
Senators hit over China trip questions

This developed as the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte criticized senators for grilling a defense witness over his trip to China, saying the issue was “irrelevant” in the ongoing impeachment trial.
Duterte spokesman Paolo Panelo said the senators’ line of questioning on Davao City assessor Jaime Adalin was “improper.”

“Even if he travels to China 10 times, that doesn’t change the fact that the property, which the prosecution said was not declared, which is covered by the transfer certificate of title ending in 0775, was actually declared in her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN),” Panelo said.
He noted that Adalin was subpoenaed to testify on the Barangay Matina Crossing property in Davao City.

“Then he will be asked for details of a trip to China that he may have forgotten about already, those details. So, I think it was unfair for him to be pressed on those questions. Like, it was also a bit insulting,” Panelo said.

Senators had questioned Adalin on the apparent discrepancies in the declared values of Duterte’s properties. They brought up Adalin’s trip to China in an effort to test his credibility. — Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Carpio: Lawmakers can discuss, oppose foreign policy
articles.summary: Nothing should stop lawmakers from issuing statements on foreign policy, retired Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Antonio Carpio said as he scored the Department of Foreign Affairs for…

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Nothing should stop lawmakers from issuing statements on foreign policy, retired Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Antonio Carpio said as he scored the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) for admonishing officials actively calling out Beijing’s encroachment on the West Philippine Sea.

“Members of Congress are free to discuss foreign policy, even oppose the foreign policy of the President and present an alternative foreign policy to the nation,” Carpio said in a statement this week.
He reminded the DFA that the Philippines “is not a dictatorship like China,” but rather “is a democracy with three independent and co-equal branches of government.”

“While the President is the chief architect of foreign policy, state policy is set by law passed by Congress which the President under the Constitution is expressly bound to ‘faithfully execute,’” he added.
He said the DFA “wants to comply with China’s demand for the ‘Philippines to strengthen its control over relevant personnel and issue a rational and unified statement on its China policy.’”
He made the remarks in reaction to DFA’s chastising unnamed officials critical of China’s sea claims and asking them to “align with the President’s policy directions.”

In its statement, the DFA said it is “regrettable that recent public commentary made by certain government officials have incorrectly merged three distinct elements: documentary evidence, public rhetoric and official diplomatic messaging.”

It said public statements against China’s provocations “risk eroding the country’s credibility in international affairs and project an image of internal division that external parties can exploit. Such actions can ultimately weaken the Philippines’ negotiating position.”

Armed Forces of the Philippines spokesman for WPS issue Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad stressed that the Philippines is not picking a fight with China but is merely standing up for the country’s maritime entitlements, sovereign rights and sovereignty.
“By merely standing up for what is rightfully and legally ours, we are not fighting any other country. That is the mandate of the DND and AFP,” he explained.

Trinidad said the AFP “would like to ensure that the next generation of Filipinos will inherit a country that is free. And all those maritime entitlements within the EEZ (exclusive economic zone) will be for them to benefit.”

“Every citizen of this country has a moral obligation to stand up for our national interest, regardless of being an individual citizen, a government employee or an elected official. The Arbitral Tribunal of 2016 is a legal landmark that upheld the maritime entitlements of the Philippines,” he added when asked about Duterte’s statements abroad that the Philippines should not be picking fights and instead assert the country’s rights over the WPS, he added.
‘Concerning’
Rep. Leila de Lima found the DFA’s message alarming.
“DFA’s most recent statement is concerning. It seems that what the DFA is saying is to leave the talking solely to them on the issue, and for everybody else to defer to their position,” De Lima said.

The House senior deputy minority leader emphasized that issuance of statements by officials – particularly from the Armed Forces of the Philippines and the Philippine Coast Guard – against China’s aggressive acts and provocations “should not cease and should not be discouraged.”
“This is crucial in promoting transparency and informing the Filipino people and the world about what is really happening in the WPS,” De Lima of the Mamamayang Liberal party-list added.

“The WPS and China are not DFA’s exclusive concern. Clearly, we must not veer away from the Philippines’ transparency initiative in the WPS, which has proven to be an effective means of countering false narratives and fake news propagated by China to amplify their baseless claims,” she pointed out.

“This issue matters to all our leaders and to every Filipino,” De Lima said. “We must all speak up for our country and our countrymen, especially those who are being harassed and deprived of their livelihoods in our territories,” she added.
“Instead of allowing ourselves to be divided on this matter, we should maintain and strengthen our united front in defending what is rightfully ours,” she maintained.
“The WPS is ours and we should not let ourselves be subservient to China,” De Lima said.
Bayan pushes diplomacy

The militant Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) has called out the Marcos administration for its “militaristic rhetoric” in dealing with China on the WPS issue, saying diplomacy should be given priority.
Bayan said that while the Philippines must assert its maritime rights, it should always purse negotiations and other peaceful ways to resolve disputes with Beijing.
“Defending our sovereignty does not require joining the US warmongering chorus. Pursuing diplomacy does not mean surrendering our sovereignty,” the group said.
The group said China’s island-building activities, incursions and harassment of Filipino fisherfolk must be opposed, but warned against turning the WPS into a flashpoint in the US-China rivalry.
“The Filipino people want neither Chinese coercion nor US aggression,” Bayan said. — Delon Porcalla, Pia Lee-Brago, Mark Ernest Villeza

MANILA, Philippines — The University of Asia and the Pacific (UA&P), together with online lending platform JuanHand, held a forum addressing school-based violence and manifestations of nihilistic violent extremism (NVE) in the Philippines.
The program drew key government officials, including DILG Secretary Jonvic Remulla and Education Secretary Sonny Angara.

“The threat of the internet and all its blessings and all its virtues and all its expansiveness in this world threatens us too as a family. And maybe there is one thing that can stop it. It is us,” Remulla said.

Meanwhile, Angara said DepEd is strengthening its safety and security protocols. Angara said he and Remulla signed a memorandum of agreement that allows barangay officials to participate in the ingress and egress of students to strengthen campus security.
Presidential Communications Office Undersecretary Claire Castro also graced the event.
In addition to government officials, representatives from several educational institutions, law enforcement units and civil society organizations attended the forum.
Providing important context regarding NVE was dark web and intelligence strategist Brian Borysewich.

He explained the workings behind NVE in the Philippines, particularly how networks of predators befriend children into performing dangerous acts. He highlighted that beyond ideology, these groomers target vulnerable children or minors, such as those with family or school problems.
Borysewich said these contexts imply that beyond the game titles, there’s a need to regulate chat boxes, the livestream and the feed.
He said children must be taught the value of consequences, and must learn that “harm has a cost before groomers and networks teach them that it has a reward.”

articles.title: More Pinoys back Leni-Raffy vs Baste-Robin – OCTA
articles.summary: A significant portion of the electorate will support Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo should she decide to again run for a national post.

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 12:00am
Leni Robredo, Raffy Tulfo, Sebastian Duterte and Robin Padilla
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — A significant portion of the electorate will support Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo should she decide to again run for a national post.

A new survey released by the OCTA Research group showed more Filipinos would support a hypothetical tandem of Robredo and Sen. Raffy Tulfo, should they face the tandem of Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte and Sen. Robin Padilla, in a one-on-one matchup.
Duterte’s name is being floated as a possible contender in the presidential race if his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, is convicted in the ongoing impeachment trial.
Based on the poll, 43 percent of the respondents said they would support a Robredo-Tulfo tandem if they face off with Baste Duterte and Padilla.
Thirty-nine percent said they would vote for a Duterte-Padilla tandem.
The remaining 18 percent either said “none” or answered “don’t know.”
OCTA pointed out that the survey was conducted over a month before Robredo reiterated her decision not to run for president in 2028, saying she lacked the “political savvy” for it.
The survey had 1,200 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus three percent.

articles.title: Defense wants 2 ICC witnesses vs Duterte, Bato dropped
articles.summary: The defense counsel of former president Rodrigo Duterte has asked trial judges of the International Criminal Court to block two of the witnesses that the prosecution intends to present in the…

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The defense counsel of former president Rodrigo Duterte has asked trial judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) to block two of the witnesses that the prosecution intends to present in the upcoming crimes against humanity trial.

In a six-page public redacted response dated Nov. 9, defense counsel Peter Haynes said the “probative value” of the prior recorded testimonies of P-1334 and P-1348 “is so limited that they should be removed from the witness list.”

“In the event that Trial Chamber III decides to admit the evidence… the defense, which does not intend to cross-examine the witnesses given the marginal value of their testimony, submits that the Chamber should not rely on those passages that directly go to the alleged acts and conduct of Mr. Duterte,” he added.

The prosecution previously asked the chamber to admit the prior recorded testimonies of the two witnesses ahead of Duterte’s trial, saying that these are “relevant” to the contextual elements of the ongoing crimes against humanity case.

In response, the defense argued that the two proposed witnesses “were both absent for almost the entire period charged under Counts 2 and 3,” referring to the charges related to killings during the Duterte administration’s deadly campaign against illegal drugs.
Count 1 involves alleged killings by the so-called Davao death squad.

“The witness expressly confirmed that she has no personal knowledge of how instructions were conveyed by Mr. Duterte, through Bato Dela Rosa, to the [REDACTED] leadership. She never saw Dela Rosa do anything of the sort, and recognized that her account is based on stories she had heard,” the defense filing read, referring to witness P-1334.
Dela Rosa, now senator, was chief of the Philippine National Police during Duterte’s drug war. He is currently in hiding due to the separate arrest warrant issued against him by the ICC.

Meanwhile, the defense pointed out the supposed lack of probative value of the testimony of witness P-1348, stressing that she “cannot speak from personal experience on the alleged quotas to kill criminals.”

“Not only is she unable to provide any details, she also seeks to fill this gap by relying on conjecture,” the defense said. “Her evidence appears to have been shaped by information obtained from news reports and social media concerning the nanlaban narrative, rather than by any direct familiarity with the events.”
The defense urged the judges to order the prosecution to drop them from the witness list.

But in the event that the chamber decides to grant the application, it requested that it only admit “those parts of the statements that relate to proof of matters other than the acts and conduct of the accused.”
The judges have yet to rule on the prosecution’s request. It was filed ahead of Duterte’s trial, which is scheduled to begin on Nov. 30.
41% see fair trial
About four in 10 Filipinos have much confidence that the ICC will conduct a fair trial against Duterte, a survey conducted by Social Weather Stations (SWS) showed.
The survey, conducted from Sept. 21 to 27, found that 41 percent of the respondents have much confidence in ICC’s fairness in the upcoming crimes against humanity trial against the ex-president.
It went down from 44 percent in a similar survey in June, but still higher than the 29 percent in March.
Meanwhile, those who had “little confidence” in the ICC’s fairness hardly moved, from 27 percent to 26 percent, while undecided respondents increased from 29 percent to 33 percent.
Based on the survey, more than half of the respondents or 55 percent follow the news on the ICC case against Duterte.
The percentage of respondents who follow news about the case significantly dropped from 72 percent in June. It was at 80 percent in November 2025.
The survey had 1,500 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus three percent, conducted months before the start of Duterte’s trial on Nov. 30.
Bato in Mindanao?
Meanwhile, the National Bureau of Investigation is validating reports that Dela Rosa is in Mindanao as authorities intensify efforts to serve an arrest warrant issued by the ICC.
NBI Director Melvin Matibag said yesterday the agency had received numerous tips about the senator’s possible whereabouts, but stressed that these were still being checked.

The senator’s possible presence in Mindanao was discussed during a closed-door coordination meeting yesterday involving the Department of Justice, Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua, BARMM ministers and governors and other Mindanao officials.
Matibag said he asked local officials to share any information that could help authorities locate Dela Rosa, without singling out any particular area.
The NBI, Matibag said, has maintained dedicated search units and continues to monitor leads through intelligence gathering, open-source information and its technical capabilities.
Meanwhile, Amnesty International Philippines urged the government to promptly execute the ICC warrant and cooperate fully with the tribunal.

“Families who lost loved ones in the ‘war on drugs’ have spent years demanding justice. They deserve action on the warrant and protection from reprisals as they pursue accountability,” Ritz Lee Santos III, section director of Amnesty International Philippines said. — Mark Ernest Villeza, Artemio Dumlao

articles.title: ‘Exceptional’ temperatures to continue until year-end
articles.summary: The streak of “exceptional” global temperatures is expected to continue through the end of the year, a new report from the United Nations weather agency revealed.

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 12:00am

Based on the World Meteorological Organization, 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record, with global average surface temperatures from January to September reaching approximately 1.47 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — The streak of “exceptional” global temperatures is expected to continue through the end of the year, a new report from the United Nations weather agency revealed.
The WMO details that the past 12 years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years topping the list.

“El Niño doesn’t add new heat to the planet. It releases heat from the ocean, which is the warmest ever measured. There is simply more heat available to release,” WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said.

The warming effect of El Niño, which has been developing since August, is expected to push temperatures higher through December, with a very strong El Niño set to unleash more extreme weather into 2027.
Around 90 percent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases is absorbed by the ocean, while glaciers continue to retreat.
The phenomenon is also raising risks for agriculture, particularly in areas facing food insecurity and where farming depends on rainfall.
The World Health Organization, for its part, has classified the expected health impacts of El Niño as a health emergency.
COP31

As countries confront worsening climate impacts, the Philippines called for stronger implementation of existing commitments, predictable climate finance and greater support for vulnerable nations at COP31, which opened Monday in Türkiye and runs until Nov. 20.
Leading the Philippine delegation, Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna stressed that climate change is already affecting Filipino communities.
“For millions of Filipino families, climate change is not a distant policy debate. It is an everyday reality affecting their livelihoods, homes and safety,” Cuna said.
He said the Philippines was pursuing international partnerships to ensure that climate pledges are backed by accessible financial and technical support.

It is also pushing for more predictable adaptation financing, direct access to loss-and-damage support and stronger implementation of commitments under the Paris Agreement, particularly for developing nations.

“From establishing the National Carbon Registry to advancing local adaptation platforms, the Philippines is showing that we are ready to lead, and we invite the global community to partner with us in securing a resilient future for all,” noted Cuna.

articles.title: Senators grill Davao accountant on VP firms
articles.summary: Senator-judges yesterday zeroed in on the relationship of defense witness, Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan, to the companies being linked to Vice President Sara Duterte in her alleged undeclared…

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Senator-judges yesterday zeroed in on the relationship of defense witness, Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan, to the companies being linked to Vice President Sara Duterte in her alleged undeclared assets and hidden wealth.

During Day 41 of the impeachment trial, Bajan testified about the P64,194.72 “salary differential” paid to Duterte from her increase in 2020 and 2021 salaries as Davao City mayor that was belatedly paid to her in 2023 when she was already Vice President.

But upon the prosecution’s cross-examination, senator-judges learned that Bajan was a partner in the accounting firm Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano, and Co. CPAs while she was already a Davao city hall employee, constituting a conflict of interest.
The prosecution pointed out the link to cast doubt on her credibility as defense witness.

The firm turned out to be an external auditor for Duterte-linked firms GenCorp Industries Inc., Metro City Chow Foods Corp., Town Times Square B, City Hall King Chow Foods Corp. and Great Jolly Times Food Corp.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian flagged Bajan’s connection to the Duterte firms because of her double job as Davao city accountant and an external auditor partner.

Sen. Francis Pangilinan pointed out Bajan became a regular employee of the Davao City Accounting Office in 2004, while she was a partner in the accounting firm. She resigned from the accounting firm only in 2015 and was appointed Davao city accountant in 2017 by the Vice President herself when Duterte was mayor.

Senator-judges were irked by Bajan’s initial hesitation to answer questions about her double job as city hall employee and accounting firm partner by feigning ignorance about her signature on the partnership’s papers.
“My patience is wearing thin. Forgive me. If you were part of an accounting firm, it’s probably difficult to forget that,” impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero said.
Sen. Raffy Tulfo warned Bajan that she could be cited in contempt for her refusal to answer the questions directly.

Tulfo compared her to the defense witness on Monday, Davao city assessor Jaime Adalin, who also irritated the senator-judges for smirking at the court while dodging questions about an all-expenses paid trip to China.

“Yesterday, the witness was laughing his ass off. This one is very evasive, feigning ignorance. Why don’t we slap them with contempt so they will have some respect for the impeachment court,” he said.
Sen. Panfilo Lacson had earlier warned witnesses that they can be cited in contempt anytime if they continue their “mockery” of the trial.

Sen. Bam Aquino, meanwhile, appealed to Bajan to just answer questions directly, saying the senator-judges were not implying that she had committed a crime, although he warned her of being in “dangerous territory” by being evasive.

Sen. Risa Hontiveros said she found it hard to believe Bajan would not remember affixing her signature in her partnership with the accounting firm, as she also cast doubt on Bajan’s ignorance on the auditing services to Duterte-linked firms.
Witness: I almost became a nun
Bajan turned emotional during the interjection of Sen. Joel Villanueva, who asked her to convince him that she had good intentions as a government official despite moonlighting in an accounting firm.
Bajan said she had earned her keep by being a hardworking city hall employee in Davao, telling the senator-judges that she almost became a nun and was grateful she entered public service instead.
Sen. Lito Lapid, for his part, said he commiserated with Bajan, who was starting to look distressed at their questions on the alleged conflict of interest.
Lapid asked her if she was being used by testifying for the defense in the Vice President’s impeachment trial, to which Bajan said no.

In her interjection, Sen. Imee Marcos took up the cudgels for the defense witness, saying she was being asked about “collateral issues” not related to her testimony about the Vice President’s salary differential.
‘Glaring discrepancies’
Meanwhile, the prosecution flagged what they described as “glaring discrepancies” in the testimony of Duterte’s witnesses regarding her alleged concealed properties.
Private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. questioned the defense’s claim that the properties in Davao City had been declared in Duterte’s statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN).
The issue first arose during the testimony of Adalin on Nov. 9, whom the defense presented to prove that a property in Matina Crossing, Davao City had been declared in Duterte’s SALN.

The prosecution maintained that the property, registered under Duterte’s husband Manases Carpio, had not been disclosed. The defense claimed, however, that it was listed under a different location description.
Tolosa said a similar issue had emerged over another property registered under Carpio’s name in Barangay San Isidro, Kaputian, Island Garden City of Samal.
During cross-examination, Tolosa established that Duterte’s 2025 SALN listed an acquisition cost of P4 million and an acquisition year of 2013 for the property cited by the defense.
But the deed of absolute sale for the property registered under Duterte’s husband showed a selling price of P3.4 million and was executed five years later on March 15, 2018.
“You will admit that the purchase price indicated here, it’s not P4 million. It’s P3.4 million?” Tolosa asked Island Garden City of Samal assessor John Kenneth Enumerables yesterday.
“Yes, correct, sir,” the witness replied.
The Samal property, covered by Transfer Certificate of Title number 142-2019013134, has an assessed value of P346,960 and a market value of P4.9 million.
“This property also, there are glaring discrepancies,” Tolosa told the court.

The disputed property forms part of the prosecution’s evidence supporting its allegation that Duterte accumulated at least P817.87 million in undeclared assets and unexplained wealth from 2022 to 2025.

Enumerables confirmed that the land titles he presented contained no annotation of a contract to sell. The property, covered by Transfer Certificate of Title No. 142-2019013134, is officially located in Barangay San Isidro, Kaputian, Island Garden City of Samal.
But the property cited by the defense in Duterte’s SALN was listed under Barangay Matanos, Kaputian. The witness earlier acknowledged that the two locations did not match.
He said he relied on the matching assessed value of P346,960 and market value of P4.9 million to link the property to Duterte’s SALN. — Delon Porcalla, Neil Jayson Servallos, Daphne Galvez

articles.title: Angelina in Manila for ASEAN Inclusive Growth Summit
articles.summary: Oscar-winning actress, filmmaker and humanitarian Angelina Jolie arrived in Manila early morning yesterday for the 2026 ASEAN Inclusive Growth Summit, where she will serve as a speaker.

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Oscar-winning actress, filmmaker and humanitarian Angelina Jolie arrived in Manila early morning yesterday for the 2026 ASEAN Inclusive Growth Summit, where she will serve as a speaker.
Jolie arrived at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 1 on Philippine Airlines flight PR103 from Los Angeles, California.
The actress will join Cambodian filmmaker Rithy Panh, who co-produced Jolie’s film “First They Killed My Father,” for a closing discussion on Cambodia, moderated by businesswoman Shamina Singh.
Filipina theater star and singer Lea Salonga and former beauty queen Kylie Verzosa are also scheduled to speak at the summit.

Broadcast journalist Rico Hizon will interview Salonga about her career and the lessons aspiring artists in the region can draw from her experience, while Versoza is expected to participate in the afternoon program, where she will discuss her ventures, including shapewear brand Solá and telehealth company &you.
Security up
As the ASEAN summit approaches, government agencies are tightening security and implementing traffic measures from Nov. 15 to 18 to ensure the safety of visiting leaders and minimize disruptions.

The Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) will deploy 1,418 personnel for traffic management and road clearing, while the Philippine Coast Guard will field 750 personnel, seven vessels and smaller boats to secure Manila Bay and summit venues.
Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. has directed the Highway Patrol Group to coordinate with the MMDA on traffic management.

The National Capital Region Police Office will also establish assistance posts along affected roads and intersections, while the Armed Forces of the Philippines, through the Presidential Security Command, will secure foreign leaders, hotels, roads and summit venues.
The MMDA urged the public to avoid designated ASEAN routes and nonessential trips.
The EDSA Busway route from Ayala to Roxas Boulevard will be converted into two lanes for authorized vehicles and convoys.
Road closures will be enforced from Nov. 15 to 18 along Atang dela Rama, Vicente Sotto, Pedro Bukaneg and Magdalena Jalandoni streets.
Roads surrounding the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City will also be designated security exclusion zones.
Motorists were advised to monitor traffic updates, take alternative routes and expect delays.
Flights disrupted
More than 300 flights, mostly to domestic destinations, will be cancelled or rescheduled due to the ASEAN Summit, the Department of Transportation announced yesterday.
Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said disruptions are expected to begin on Nov. 14, when heads of state are expected to start arriving, and continue through their departures after the summit.
Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific and AirAsia Philippines have announced flight disruptions, affecting routes to Macau, Caticlan, Iloilo and Tacloban, among others.

Malacañang, meanwhile, defended the clearing of vendors, street dwellers and small businesses along major roads, saying the measures are necessary to ensure the safety of visiting officials. — Andrew Ronquillo, Rainier Allan Ronda, Elijah Felice Rosales, Josiah Antonio, Michael Punongbayan, Mark Ernest Villeza, Evelyn Macairan, Helen Flores

articles.title: US files request for Quiboloy extradition – DOJ

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — The United States government has asked a court in Makati City to extradite detained pastor Apollo Quiboloy and two others so they can face various charges against them.
