articles.title: Defense witness was partner at accounting firm for VP Sara business assets
articles.summary: A witness for the defense in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte used to be partner at the accounting firm for firms that are declared assets of Duterte and Mans Carpio.

blocks.text: A witness for the defense in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday was a partner at the accounting firm for companies that are declared assets of Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio.

Private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia said that Davao City Accountant Vengeline Bahan used to be a partner at Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co., CPAs, citing that her signature as partner is reflected in the firm’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) records, including the 2003 Articles of Partnership.
Divinangracia asked Bahan to confirm her signature as one of the firm’s partners based on SEC records, but Bahan could not give an answer.
"Pirma niyo ho yan, tama ba? Hindi niyo rin po ba makikilala ang inyong pirma?, Ms. Bahan, Divinagracia said.
(Can you confirm that this is your signature? Can you not recognize your signature?)
Bahan was still not giving any answer at this point and kept on flipping pages of the documents.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero cautioned Bahan against flipping pages, saying there is only one signature page.
Divinagracia responded by saying “We would just like to put it on record that this witness seems to refuse to answer or is hesitating to answer the question.”
Escudero then pressed Bahan to answer by asking if she is unfamiliar with the document.
Bahan answered in the affirmative.

When Divinagracia asked Bahan to confirm if Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co., CPAs is the same accounting firm of GenCorp. Industries Inc., Metro City Chow Foods Corporation, Times Square B, City Hall King Chow, Chinese Gen B, Carpio Lawyers, Davao New Royal Taipan and Great Jolly Times Food Corporation as stated in these firms’ General Information Sheet (GIS) submitted to the SEC, Bahan said she could not recall such involvement of her former firm.
"You can refer to the General Information Sheets (GIS) to help you out,” Divinagracia said.
Defense counsel Lindon Bacquel objected to the question, but this was overruled by Escudero.
Bahan responded, “Hindi ko po ma-remember.” (I cannot recall.)

Bahan, however, confirmed that Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co., CPAs original Articles of Partnership dated 2003 and amended Articles of Partnership in 2015, there is only one SEC registration number for the said firm.
“Pareho po [ang SEC registration] number,” Bahan said.
Escudero then asked Bahan if she ever served as external accountant of Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co., CPAs, to which Bahan replied, “Hindi ko po ma-remember your honor, sa tagal na po.”
(I cannot remember, your honor. It has been too long.)

Bahan, however, confirmed that she was a partner of the accounting firm Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co., CPAs and left the firm in 2015 when she was confronted by the same documents, including her affidavit of withdrawal as firm’s partner in 2015, by Senator-judge Joel Villanueva.
Villanueva read a portion of Bahan’s affidavit which read “I resigned in the partnership effective August 1, 2015 due to personal reasons."
“Sigurado po ako ito ang pirma niyo dahil ito ang nasa official record,” Villanueva said.
“Para sabihin niyo na hindi niyo maalala, mahirap ho kami makumbinsi sa ganun. You are not contesting this [affidavit of withdrawal]?,” Villanueva added.
Bahan answered in the affirmative. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Jinggoy Estrada had P1.6 billion in budget insertions, says witness
articles.summary: Senator Jinggoy Estrada inserted over P1.6 billion worth of projects in the budget of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in 2025, a witness told the Sandiganbayan on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published November 10, 2026 6:46pm
Senator Jinggoy Estrada inserted over P1.6 billion worth of projects in the budget of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in 2025, a witness told the Sandiganbayan on Tuesday.
According to the judicial affidavit of witness DPWH Programming Division Chief Engr. Peter Paul Cortez, these budget insertions were spread across 16 projects.

Testifying before the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division, Cortez said that these insertions were in the 1st and 3rd District Engineering Offices of Bulacan. He also alleged that there were budget insertions at the National Capital Region office.
The DPWH employee also said that these projects appeared in the 2025 General Appropriations Act (GAA) without appearing in the National Expenditure Program.
Cortez reportedly found out about Estrada’s projects because this was part of the list given to him by the late DPWH undersecretary Catalina Cabral.
Cabral reportedly sent the list to his office so that it could be encoded into the DPWH’s database.
Estrada is currently being tried for a P573 million plunder case in relation to the flood control scam.

Billions of pesos were allegedly funneled through bogus flood control projects, with officials and lawmakers allegedly pocketing millions in the process. Estrada is among those who have been accused of being part of the scam. –NB, GMA News

image.caption: The incident reportedly included an elite police officer trained in handling explosives and K-9 handlerImage: Juan Vega/Europa Press/IMAGO

blocks.text: A national police officer was killed in Oviedo, Spain on Tuesday following an explosion in the Villafria neighborhood. Another is being treated for serious wounds in a nearby hospital.

According to local media, the officers were responding to an escalating dispute between two local families in which a woman was shot by a man early in the morning. She is reportedly expected to recover, though it remains unclear what prompted the attack.
The two officers — a member of the elite TEDAX explosives unit and a canine handler — approached a suspicious backpack at the scene, which then detonated before it could be neutralized.
Police union JUPOL expressed its "deep sorrow and dismay" over the incident.

The area surrounding Rafael Urrusti Street has been cordoned off. Spanish daily El Pais reported that Oviedo Mayor Alfredo Canteli is heading to the scene to try and settle some of the confusion surrounding the attacks.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan suspends Martin Romualdez over plunder case
articles.summary: 'The court issued a resolution ordering the suspension pendente lite of former speaker Ferdinand Martin Gomez Romualdez for a period of 90 days from receipt of the resolution,' says the Sandiganbayan…

blocks.text: ARRAIGNMENT. Former House speaker Martin Romualdez during his arraignment on September 16, 2026.
Aaron Favila/AP/Sandiganbayan pool

'The court issued a resolution ordering the suspension pendente lite of former speaker Ferdinand Martin Gomez Romualdez for a period of 90 days from receipt of the resolution,' says the Sandiganbayan 3rd Division
MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan 3rd Division ordered the suspension of former speaker Martin Romualdez due to his plunder case related to the flood control scandal.

“The court issued a resolution ordering the suspension pendente lite of former speaker Ferdinand Martin Gomez Romualdez for a period of 90 days from receipt of the resolution. The resolution orders the former speaker to cease and desist from the functions of his office or any other office,” 3rd Division Executive Clerk Dennis Pulma said on Tuesday, November 10.
Romualdez is facing plunder, a non-bailable offense, due to alleged P7.44-billion in kickbacks from government projects.

The Office of the Ombudsman filed the plunder charge against him with the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan on September 7. On the same day, the 3rd Division issued a warrant of arrest against Romualdez and ordered his detention.
The lawmaker, a first cousin of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., has been detained in the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas since September 14.

Under Section 5 of Republic Act No. 7080 or the Plunder Law, any public officer charged with the case “whatever stage of execution and mode of participation, is pending in court, shall be suspended from office.”
Romualdez is Leyte 1st District representative – Rappler.com

articles.title: David Jones’s finances were reviewed and restructuring flagged months before it fell into administration
articles.summary:
Department store group kept buying new products and fell months behind in payments to some brands despite discussions with administrators

  • Get our

blocks.text: David Jones’s administrators have revealed they reviewed its finances six months ago and discussed restructuring the retailer three months before it fell into administration.

The new timeline raises questions over the department store group’s decision to keep buying new products and fall months behind in payments to some brands before it revealed last Thursday it could not pay its debts.
The process could leave unsecured creditors with substantial losses, with unpaid product suppliers and shoppers holding unredeemed gift vouchers most at risk.
The McGrathNicol administrators invited David Jones’s creditors, which also include employees and landlords, to attend a 17 November meeting in its first circular on Tuesday.

McGrathNicol’s team said it had been engaged by the lawyers for David Jones’s owners, Anchorage Capital, as early as April 2026 to analyse some of the department store group’s financial information, though it said it did not directly advise the group or review its ability to pay debts.

By July, David Jones’s group director, Simon Woodhouse, and its biggest lender, Hilco, met McGrathNicol to discuss David Jones’s financial performance, “potential restructuring” and to form a working group to regularly discuss the issues.
But the administrators said Woodhouse left the meeting when the “potential restructuring” was discussed and no working group was formed.

At the same time, David Jones was putting small suppliers on tiered and extended payment terms, with brands forced to accept ever-deeper discounts to get faster payments, according to several businesses contacted by Guardian Australia.
McGrathNicol said it did not discuss David Jones’s dire financial position again until 22 October, when Woodhouse asked them to help plan a for potential voluntary administration.

It said Woodhouse and others held another five meetings in the following fortnight before a series of briefings last Wednesday, the day before the administration was announced, as the company negotiated with its landlords and prepared for collapse.
McGrathNicol said David Jones Group paid it $1m upfront that day to run the administration. It told creditors it expected to access another $3m to $4m of funding.
The first creditors’ meeting will take place on 17 November, McGrathNicol said.

A second meeting is typically required six weeks later but McGrathNicol said it would apply to have that delayed another three months, or to early April 2027, to give it more time to sell the business or raise more funds.

The letter did not offer more detail on David Jones’s financial situation, or how long it had been insolvent. McGrathNicol said it had asked the company’s directors to prepare a report on their business, property and financial circumstances.
FTI Consulting, which is running David Jones’s day-to-day business during the administration process, on Monday said the company had remained fully operational.
Anchorage Capital, David Jones and Hilco were contacted for comment on Tuesday night.

articles.title: Fact check: Online disinformation rife after Krakow mass shooting
articles.summary: Fake and AI-manipulated images spread online in the hours after the Krakow attack, fueling false narratives about the mass shooting. DW Fact Check examined what's real, and what isn't.

image.caption: The shock after the deadly shootings in Krakow runs deep. On social media, this moment is being used to spread misinformationImage: Beata Zawrzel/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A gunman killed six people in a shooting spree in Krakow's Old Town on Saturday, before being shot and detained by police. The gunman, who is also suspected of killing three family members before the attack, later died in hospital.
On Monday, Poland's national prosecutor's office announced a formal investigation.

Nevertheless, much is still unknown about the details of the crime, leaving social media users to fill the information vacuum with fake images of the attacker and alleged screenshots of his online profile. DW Fact Check breaks down the developing story.
Are these genuine images of the attacker?
Claim: A viral picture has been circulating on social media claiming to be the real image of the suspected attacker.
DW Fact Check: Fake
In the post, the image is posted with the caption, "[…] The perpetrator of the attack in Krakow is a 25-year-old Polish citizen, Polish police have reported. The death toll has reached six. (…)".
But the unusual sharpness of this picture raises doubt of its authenticity. It is difficult to imagine capturing such a clear image in a chaotic situation.

blocks.caption: The footage from X posts about the alleged shooter in Krakow is said to supposedly show the face of the shooter lying on the ground after the attack in Krakow. The face has been altered multiple times with AIImage: X

blocks.text: DW checked the image using two different AI detectors. Hive Moderation identified it as 99.5% AI-generated, while Google's SynthID Detector confirmed that it contains a SynthID watermark, indicating that it was generated or edited using Google's AI technology.
In our research we found several versions of the suspect image circulating online, most looking very similar. We also found a number of images and videos showing the attack.
Although DW cannot independently verify the footage, it shares similarities in terms of the people and background with some original images published by picture agencies.
It appears the AI-generated images may have been created using this footage as a reference. Some of the posts sharing these images have also been labeled as AI-generated.

One important thing to understand is that AI cannot sharpen a blurry image with correct details or recover details that are not visible in an original photograph. It can generate plausible details based on the surrounding visual information, but these are essentially guesses, not exact reproductions of what was actually there.
More about this and how users used sharpening AI tools here.

blocks.caption: Was the shooter really a supporter of Ukraine? This claim is supposedly backed up by this picture of a post in a Telegram channelImage: X

blocks.text: Did the shooter sympathize with Ukraine?

Claim: "Michal Oksinski, the terrorist from Krakow who also killed his parents and sister, had a Telegram account with the Ukrainian flag. On November 3, he wrote 'Thanks, Dad, for the gun', posting this photo of himself wearing the Ukrainian flag insignia," an X user wrote in a post viewed more than 700,000 times.

This Telegram channel is almost certainly inauthentic. The account allegedly posted a photo on November 3, showing the attacker holding a gun, standing in front of a television and a Ukrainian insignia on the wall.
Another post on November 4 simply reads, "11/7/2026", the date of the attack. Both of these posts were edited on November 8, after the suspect had been apprehended.
DW verified on the Telegram app by hovering over the posts to show the edit history. The channel's photo, a Ukrainian flag, was also edited after the attack took place.

blocks.caption: Fake: Digital AI tools indicate the image was 99% likely to have been created using AIImage: Hivemoderation.com

blocks.text: This is a common disinformation tactic — fake accounts will edit old posts and pictures in the days after a breaking news event to give the appearance that they've predicted or announced the event in advance.

Further proof: in Poland, the date is written first, not the month. And the photo of the alleged attacker itself is almost certainly AI-generated. HIVE Moderation said it was 99.9% likely to be created with AI.
Does the attacker have links to a group that operated in Ukraine?

Claim: "#BREAKING: The attacker in Poland had a full arsenal in this trunk! He also has forward observation group patches, an American military company active in Ukraine," reads an X post viewed nearly 100,000 times. The attached photo of the supposed "arsenal" in the trunk has been shared by several other accounts.
DW Fact Check: False
The attached photo claims to show the attacker's car with a trunk full of guns, ammunition, a helmet and a military vest.
The vest in the trunk of the car features a symbol supposedly connected to the Forward Observations Group, an American tactical training lifestyle brand that has traveled to and operated in Ukraine.

blocks.caption: This is a photo of a trunk full of weapons — but this picture doesn't show the alleged attacker's carImage: X

blocks.text: The patch, however, is the Old Roger flag, a symbol commonly used in military circles. The Forward Observations Group logo is a variationof this symbol, featuring a horned skeleton holding a gun, not an hourglass.

This is also not the attacker's car from the scene of the crime. This license plate is registered with the Krakow police, indicating they likely collected evidence from the crime scene and moved it to this car.
Little details like these can help separate fact from fiction, especially in a rapidly evolving story like the Krakow shooting.
Daniel Ebertz contributed to this article.

articles.title: [Kasalikasan] Here we go again: Climate talks kick off in Turkey
articles.summary: 'The world has been addressing climate change together for over three decades, yet the numbers are still alarming'

blocks.text: Hello!
The annual United Nations Climate Change Conference opened Monday, November 9, in Antalya, Turkey — now the 31st session (COP31) since talks started in Berlin, Germany, in 1995.

The world has been addressing climate change together for over three decades, yet the numbers are still alarming. According to the World Meteorological Organization’s (WMO) State of the Climate Update released also Monday:

items: 2026 will be one of four warmest years on record.

With the “off the charts” Super El Niño underway, temperatures are likely to rise further. “It is different from any El Niño that we have monitored,” warned WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, urging countries to prepare for an even warmer 2027. In the Philippines, senators are urging President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity in Super El Niño-hit areas.
Ocean heat is the highest on record for the 10th consecutive year. Sea level has also reached a record high, increasing risks for 900 million people living along low-lying coasts.

Saulo said during a COP31 briefing that the world is “supercharging our weather…. Heatwaves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for. The human and economic cost is unacceptably high.”

blocks.text: Lest we forget, we’re starting this year’s climate talks after a disappointing COP30 outcome that promised to triple adaptation finance by 2035 but omitted any mention of the fossil fuels that drive climate change in the first place. No wonder former leaders and climate experts had two years ago criticized the annual climate talks as “no longer fit for purpose” and needing reform. (WATCH: What happened at COP30?)

But I’ve covered these talks closely for the last five years, and no matter how disappointing each conference ends, tens of thousands still participate because it remains the only platform for the world to negotiate climate change solutions. And as long as countries keep showing up, the hope continues.
For instance, the Philippines is finally coming to Antalya with an updated nationally determined contribution, incomplete it may be.

This year’s COP is also putting the spotlight on the world’s oceans — fitting, considering how the ocean absorbs 90% of the excess heat trapped in the Earth’s climate system by excess greenhouse gases. And aside from world leaders, communities that are oceans apart come together at COPs to share best practices and solutions, especially those that face similar challenges.

“No COP is a silver bullet,” said UN climate chief Simon Stiell in his opening remarks on Monday. “No single conference can bridge the chasm between science and reality. We must deal with the world as it is, not as we might wish it to be. Every recent COP has delivered strides forward. This one must too.”
Let’s get to work.

We’re doing things differently this year: follow Rappler’s coverage of COP31 high-level events in the Environment and Science chat room of our MUNI app. Here’s what happened on Day 1. For more stories, bookmark this page.
Till the Tuesday after next!
Here are other stories from our cluster that you shouldn’t miss:
Lean Alejandro and climate justice: Why Lidy Nacpil now believes in living for a cause
The tree Quezon planted, and Bacolod nearly forgot

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine engage in 4-hour session on first day of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.summary: Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington made another push to end the war that followed Moscow's all-out invasion of its…

image.caption: U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, right, speaks as his colleague Jared Kushner, left, and NATO official Alexus Grynkewich listen, at the beginning of talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates on Tuesday. (Altaf Qadri/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington made another push to end the war that followed Moscow's all-out invasion of its neighbour nearly five years ago.
Warring sides say they want peace as U.S. pushes for a resolution to the war that began in February 2022

The first day of talks in Abu Dhabi concluded after nearly four hours, the RIA Novosti news agency said. They are expected to resume on Wednesday, according to the press office of the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine.
There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks took place against a backdrop of new long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.
Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said.
Russia attacked 10 ‌Ukrainian regions overnight, hitting ​five major ​energy substations that ​transmit electricity between ⁠regions, ⁠Ukrainian ‌Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi ⁠said on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Russia's Ministry of Defence said that its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight above eight Russian regions, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014.
Firefighters work at the site of a residential building hit by a Russian jet drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Tuesday. (Reuters)

The U.S. is renewing a push to end the war between Moscow and Kyiv after three rounds of negotiations earlier this year. The conflict, Europe's biggest since the Second World War, began after Russia's all-out invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the talks "constructive and quite substantive" and said they had included humanitarian and security issues.

items: Putin pushes the myth of Russian invincibility, seemingly to set his terms for peace

blocks.text: "The release of prisoners [of war] is a priority. They spoke in detail about the substance of security guarantees for Ukraine and the foundations for ensuring these guarantees function over the long term," he posted on X.
Security guarantees also were discussed, he added during an appearance at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark.
European diplomats meet with U.S. envoys

U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner who, along with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, is trying to broker a settlement, said he believed there were "some good ideas how to bridge" the differences between the two sides.

Trump, whose stance on the war has varied, with more frequent criticisms of Kyiv than the Kremlin in recent weeks, must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections. Democrats could demand more support for Ukraine.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in an interview with ZDF television on Monday night that he didn't have "overly high expectations" from the talks.
How involved is Melania Trump in the push for peace in Ukraine?
NATO commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who was also present at the talks, pointed to "some great progress in the past in a military-to-military dialogue in a trilateral format."
Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service who leads Kyiv's delegation, thanked the U.S. for its efforts to end Russia's invasion.
"Our people are waiting to end this war. And we hope that we will achieve the lasting peace for Ukraine," he said.

items: Putin pushes the myth of Russian invincibility, seemingly to set his terms for peace

blocks.text: Umerov said the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission.
Russia has objected to the Europeans' involvement in the three-way talks but said EU representatives could join at a later stage.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, expressed hope the meeting "will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine."
LISTEN | Reuters correspondent Dan Peleschuk on Ukraine conscription controversies:
Front Burner21:55Ukrainian conscription in the crosshairs
Russia and Ukraine hold to their divergent demands
The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal to end the full-scale war, now nearing its five-year mark.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson — the four regions that Moscow illegally annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.
This is how residents of the besieged town of Oleshky stayed alive

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles. He has warned that Russia will achieve its goals by force if Kyiv refuses to meet its conditions for peace.

Zelenskyy rejects Putin's demands to voluntarily cede territory that Russia hasn't been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy also rejects any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, in Moscow, said Tuesday that it would be wiser to discuss ⁠the outlines of the future security ‌architecture in Europe first, and then a ​ceasefire in Ukraine.

items: Kite flying in Ukraine: One N.S. veteran's mission to help children in a war zone

blocks.text: While the ground battles have morphed into a war of attrition along the 1,200-kilometre front line, Russia and Ukraine have ramped up their long-range strikes with drones and missiles.

Russia has intensified its air campaign against Ukraine's power grid, seeking to weaken the country's resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine's shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has escalated its drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

articles.title: Parañaque clears Baclaran roads of street vendors for ASEAN Summit
articles.summary: The Parañaque City government clarifies that vendors will be allowed to return after the summit, provided they maintain an orderly setup

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Parañaque City government has cleared roads surrounding Baclaran Church of street vendors as the Philippines hosts the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

In a statement released on Sunday, November 8, the city government said street vendors are “temporarily prohibited” from operating along Roxas Boulevard and its service roads, from Redemptorist Road to Quirino Avenue, as well as the road beneath the Light Rail Transit (LRT) line. The restriction is in effect from November 2 to 20.

“Pansamantala lamang na ipinagbabawal ang ambulant vendors sa mga lugar na saklaw ng clearing. Kinausap sila at humingi kami ng paumanhin at pag-unawa bago pa sinimulan ito,” the city government said.
(The ban on ambulant vendors in areas covered by the clearing operations is only temporary. We spoke with the vendors and apologized, asking for their understanding before the operations began.)
The city government clarified that vendors would be allowed to return after the summit, provided they maintain an orderly setup.

The local government is also planning to relocate the vendors to the Baclaran Gateway Market, near the water channel across Redemptorist Church. The structure, still under construction, is intended to serve as their permanent area for selling goods.
Some vendors, however, are already struggling to make ends meet after being barred from selling along Baclaran’s streets.

Malyn Antonio, a single mother of three, said she continues to sell tempered glass phone screen protectors in Baclaran despite the prohibition. But business has been slow. After working from noon to midnight, she earned only P130.
Her earnings were not even enough to provide one of her children with school allowance, forcing the child to miss classes.

“Nakakaawa na pumasok tapos nakikita niya ‘yung mga estudyante na kumakain, nagre-recess siya wala,” Antonio said. (It’s heartbreaking for her to come to school and see other students eating during recess when she has nothing.)
The city government said affected vendors would receive financial assistance.
Antonio hopes the assistance will be sufficient and distributed soon.
Another affected vendor, Norania Balayo, criticized the government’s decision to drive vendors away from the streets.
“Ang gobyerno natin ngayon mapagkunwari na walang mahirap sa Pilipinas. Dapat kung ano mayroon sa Pilipinas, pinapakita nila sa taong bayan [o] ibang nasyon,” Balayo said.
(Our government today is pretending that there are no poor people in the Philippines. They should show the public and other nations the realities of life in the country.)
On Tuesday, November 10, city officials also towed around 50 electric tricycles (e-trikes) plying Roxas Boulevard.
Under the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority’s Memorandum Circular No. 4, Series of 2024, e-trikes are prohibited from using national roads, including Roxas Boulevard.

blocks.caption: TOWING. Parañaque City officials impound e-trikes plying Roxas Boulevard on November 10, 2026. Photo by Patrick Cruz/Rappler

blocks.text: City officials told reporters that owners can reclaim their impounded e-trikes after the ASEAN Summit.
Meanwhile, workers from the city engineering office were also seen repainting the walls surrounding Baclaran Church.

blocks.caption: ASEAN 2026. A worker paints a vandalized wall in Baclaran ahead of the ASEAN Summit on November 10, 2026. Photo by Patrick Cruz/Rappler

articles.title: DR Congo: 66 soldiers sentenced to death for cowardice in conflict with FRN rebels
articles.summary: Dozens of defendants were put on trial over accusations that they abandoned their posts and refused to follow direct orders.

image.caption: This is not the first time Congolese troops have been sentenced to death for abandoning their postsImage: Alain Uaykani/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: Some 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in DR Congo on charged of cowardice, mutiny, and failure to obey orders. The sentence was handed down by the Goma Garrison Military Court.

At least 71 members of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) were arrested in several separate incidents related to the fierce fighting between the military and rebel groups near the country's borders with Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi.

They were arrested on allegations of abandoning their posts or running away from clashes with FRN rebels. Prosecutors had sought capital punishment for 70 of the defendants, while asking for a 10-year jail term for an intelligence officer. The court, however, acquitted four defendants,

Major Dieudonné Kasereka, head of communications for FARDC in the affected region, said that the charges were necessary to reinforce discipline in the country's embattled North Kivu and South Kivu regions.
What is the FRN?
The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation is an umbrella group of rebels that also includes the March 23 Movement (M23) and Alliance River Congo (AFC).
The group's origins can be traced back to the Rwandan genocide in 1994 and the ensuing ethnic conflict, as it emerged from the Congolese Tutsi militias of the time.

It is led by former DR Congo President Joseph Kabila. When current President Felix Tshisekedi came into power in 2019, Kabila found himself increasingly ostracized politically and went into self-imposed exile in an area occupied my what was then M23. Further complicating the conflict is the involvement of the FDLR rebel group, an ethnic Rwandan Hutu militia also active in South Kivu.

Although Rwanda's strongman president Paul Kagame denied involvement in the conflict, both DR Congo and many in the international community held that evidence of Rwandan involvement was clear. Indeed, Rwanda was involved in the 2025 US-brokered peace deal — which was seen as mostly serving US economic interests and doing little to resolve the long-running conflict.

Earlier this year, the United Nations condemned FRN and Rwandan soldiers for "murder, torture and other ill-treatment, corporal punishment, forced unlawful recruitment and abusive labor, and use of child soldiers."

articles.title: Pulling the trigger: Caidic praises UE as Warriors fight for lost culture, pride
articles.summary: UE team consultant Allan Caidic, the Philippine basketball legend nicknamed the ‘Triggerman,’ hopes the Red Warriors will ‘erase all doubts’ after their breakthrough win

blocks.text: RELIEF. Toper Lagat (No. 4) and the UE Red Warriors end a 30-game losing streak after outlasting Adamson in the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament.
UAAP
UE team consultant Allan Caidic, the Philippine basketball legend nicknamed the ‘Triggerman,’ hopes the Red Warriors will ‘erase all doubts’ after their breakthrough win

items: The UE Red Warriors achieved a historic 53-47 victory over Adamson, ending a 30-game losing streak in UAAP men's basketball.
Team consultant Allan Caidic emphasized the importance of this win for the players' morale and confidence, hoping it would help them believe in their ability to compete.
Despite facing challenges with roster changes, the team is motivated to restore their winning culture and improve under the guidance of Caidic and new head coach Paulo Hubalde.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – For the first time in more than two years, the UE Red Warriors can call themselves winners in UAAP men’s basketball following a historic 53-47 win over Adamson on Saturday, November 7.

Although making “history” in this case is far from what the proud, 18-time champion program was used to back in their glory days, history is history nonetheless as the Red Warriors ended a massive 30-game losing streak dating back to October 2024 in Season 87.

When the buzzer rang across the Araneta Coliseum, there was no dry eye nor quiet mouth from the ranks of the UE players and coaching staff, including new head coach Paulo Hubalde and team consultant Allan Caidic.
Plenty of legends have come and gone through UE’s halls and played proudly for the red and white, but Caidic is on another tier of his own.

One of the greatest stars in Filipino basketball history, the “Triggerman” is UE culture incarnate. With three UAAP titles, three UAAP MVPs, five PBA titles, and eight PBA All-Star selections, Caidic treated wins as par for the course and always set his sights on the bigger picture.
Yet on that fateful Saturday afternoon, he was not one to dismiss the value of what a solitary victory can do to a program, particularly one that has been struggling the way his alma mater is.

“I hope this win will erase all doubts with the players, and they feel that they can actually compete and we can win games,” Caidic said after the game, where he proudly raised his fist with the rest of the squad while singing the “Pamantasan Ka Naming Mahal”school hymn.

“That’s important for the players coming into next year, and for our last three games. If we can play the way we did, holding [Adamson] to 47 points and 17% shooting, it’s a big credit to the players themselves. This is a great morale boost. They just have to believe in themselves.”

Despite UE dealing with multiple star departures and transfers over the years that all but gutted the roster to unheralded prospects, the next men up have fought for the red and white day in and day out like new league-leading scorer Toper Lagat and Mo Tañedo.

Although Tañedo was not wrong in mentioning in the postgame presser that UE has fallen into a losing culture, Caidic was adamant in fighting for the culture they have lost — a culture that struck fear to the rest of the UAAP teams upon seeing the letters “UE” on their schedules.

“I challenged them the other day, especially the third- and second-year players. I told them ‘Do you want to go your entire career without a win?’ If we were swept this year, they would have gone 0-28. Others have gone longer, so that’s about 0-34,” the legend continued.

“So I really told them we have to stop the bleeding. The effort is there and you can see it, but you just see the inexperience. These players were just relievers last year, or didn’t even play at all. So it’s really a process, and slowly they have been able to adapt.”

Lagat, in fact, just averaged 6.8 points in UAAP Season 88, while Tañedo normed 2.5 points in a roster dominated by Precious Momowei, John Abate, and Wello Lingolingo — all of whom are now either out of collegiate basketball or playing elsewhere.

Caidic understands that nurturing this program in this current state of constant upheaval is a whole different challenge than just drilling the Xs and Os on the sideline, which is why he is even more motivated to bring out the best in every single player, regardless of results.

“I just have to keep on pushing them and lifting them, because these are not professional players whom you can tell off to adjust after just one talk. These are kids whom you have to guide and advise to be consistent,” Caidic continued.

“They’re all good kids. They follow, they work hard in practice, and you can really see prior to this game, that they have been really improving. A few of our games have come close to winning, in fact. They just really have to believe in themselves and work hard consistently.”
The UE Red Warriors are a legendary, championship-laden program. The UE Red Warriors are also one of the most prominent losing programs in modern UAAP history.
Two things can be true at once, but what matters is what the program’s players wish to be known for.
If Saturday’s game and their recent outings were any indicators, these new-age UE Red Warriors are certainly sick and tired of all the negativity.
That’s all the motivation they need. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security
articles.summary: Huang, who is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, is far more important to the future of the world order than other tech bosses.

blocks.text: Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared.
Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.
Both are innovators revered in the tech world. However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models.

In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.
Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.
I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.
It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200.

An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.
He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case.

"President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."
He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders.
However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles.
Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement.
The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.

He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.
Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern".
He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".
What does this show us?

At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views.
More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.
Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy.
Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health.

It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

articles.title: US, Russia and Ukraine hold trilateral talks aimed at ending war – Europe live
articles.summary:
Talks in Abu Dhabi are first substantive negotiations in months focusing on ending the conflict which has raged for more than four years

Donald Trump has said that Ukraine would like be…

blocks.text: Zelenskyy says Kyiv in strengthened position for talks as officials seek end to Russia-Ukraine war
We are restarting our Europe live blog ahead of the US-led trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi that seek an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on the eve of the talks that Ukrainian battlefield successes were strengthening Kyiv’s position in negotiations.

The ⁠three-sided talks between Ukrainian, Russian and ⁠US negotiators ​are to open on Tuesday and will be the first substantive talks since February aimed at ending the war, which has raged on for more than four-and-a-half years.

“Ukrainian forces are currently genuinely strengthening Ukraine’s negotiating position,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address on Monday. “Every task that is fully accomplished – every defensive operation that ⁠increases Ukraine’s strength and delivers results – strengthens Ukraine and, above all, strengthens us in negotiations.”

blocks.caption: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Russian forces have been suffering heavy losses recently in the war. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner (who is also Donald Trump’s son-in-law) are to lead the American delegation at the talks, which are scheduled for two ⁠days. In Washington, ⁠Trump said on Monday that the US was seeing ​a “very strong inclination” towards ending Russia’s war, and that both sides were “tired of fighting”.

A US official said security guarantees for Ukraine would be a central topic for the discussions, including the potential for Kyiv to be granted a Nato-style article 5 defence, which protects member states in case of an attack. Any territorial agreement would probably come at the end of negotiations once other items were agreed upon, including a postwar security architecture, the official said.

But Ukraine and Russia have both been adamant about territory, with neither side willing to make any major concessions during previous rounds of diplomacy. Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, wants to obtain all of eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region.

European officials, ⁠including from France, Germany and the European Commission, ⁠will not directly take part in negotiations, as per Russia’s insistence. But instead the Ukrainian delegation, led by foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, will meet separately to brief their European allies on progress.
Allow content provided by a third party?

This article includes content hosted on platform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

The two US envoys met Ukrainian and European officials in Abu Dhabi ahead of the trilateral talks this morning. “Our key priorities are ending the fighting, securing reliable postwar security guarantees, ensuring Ukraine’s economic recovery and development, and taking humanitarian steps,” Umerov wrote in a social media post.

European officials, who have been largely excluded from peace talks, wanted to be involved directly in the talks amid concerns the US administration could try to force through a deal favourable to Russia. Stick with us as we bring you the latest developments from the negotiations and other Europe-related news.
Key events

items: 28m agoZelenskyy says Kyiv in strengthened position for talks as officials seek end to Russia-Ukraine war

blocks.caption: Andrew Roth

blocks.text: Andrew Roth
Donald Trump has said that Ukraine would like be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape“.

After meeting with Kremlin advisor Kirill Dmitriev last week, Trump said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.

“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump ​had vowed to end the conflict when he took office in January 2025 but has failed in his goal by all accounts.  Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: In 2021, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.

“We have to build something new that works today… Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war,” said the US administration official.

The content of those proposals are not clear yet, although the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed on Monday “there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look”. “We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he added.

articles.title: Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh after two years in exile
articles.summary:
Hasina fled to India in 2024 after mass uprising. She faces death penalty upon return

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi

blocks.text: Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister of Bangladesh applied for a fresh passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She fled over the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.

Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her deadly crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.

Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had returned to the country in anticipation.

On Monday, a UK lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina, wrote to the Bangladesh high commission requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Hasina has rejected the charges of mass murder and crimes against humanity and claimed the tribunal who convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.

Since Hasina’s conviction, Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government – which was very close to Hasina while she was in power – has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.

This week, the Bangladesh government have said that as a “terrorist”, Hasina will only be allowed to return under an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty. The chief prosecutor of the tribunal who sentenced Hasina condemned her announcement to return as a “nothing but a political stunt”.
Despite her conviction and the banning of her party, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many who have been driven underground.

Analysts believe her decision to return, despite the risk of arrest, is driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly-elected government, led by prime minister Tarique Rahman. They were brought to power after in February in Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.
Since then, the government has struggled with inflation and recent protests that shut down garment factories, which Awami League hopes to use to its political advantage.

Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite the threat of arrest and jail. Many of those who were close to Hasina over her 15 years in power have faced severe criminal charges since the fall of her government and have been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.

“All of us are planning to go back. Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is also based in India.

Some senior party figures have already gone back in recent months, including former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. Ruhi was immediately arrested by police after returning in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder committed during the 2024 uprising.
“There are serious threats and dangers, but our cadres and leaders are confident and prepared to return to our people,” the leader said.
During their years in exile, Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.

Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press she affirmed her decision to go back. “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” she said.

articles.title: Descendants say reviving Japanese Canadian veterans' Legion rights historical wrong

image.caption: Yoshihiro Kamachi is pictured in Vancouver, B.C., on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Kamachi is a veteran himself, and his uncle served in the First World War. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
After internment forced its closure, a Legion that served Japanese Canadian veterans of the First World War is being resurrected.
Before internment forced its closure, this branch served Japanese Canadians who fought for Canada

As Remembrance Day approaches, members of Royal Canadian Legion-British Columbia Japanese Canadian Branch No. 9 — many of whom are descendants of the Japanese Canadian veterans it served — say joining the long-lost Legion is a way to honour their relatives' memory.

The attack on Pearl Harbor prompted Canada to label its residents of Japanese heritage as "enemy aliens," and thousands were forced into internment camps, while their possessions were seized and sold without consent.
Members of Branch No. 9 seek to spread the word about the Legion to right a historical wrong while educating the public about the veterans' contributions.

items: Japanese immigrants fought for Canada during WW I while denied the right to vote

blocks.text: "I think he would be very happy about it," said new Branch No. 9 president David Mitsui, reflecting on his grandfather.
He is the grandson of Masumi Mitsui, a decorated veteran of Vimy Ridge and Hill 70 who headed the branch before it closed.
Community historian Debbie Jiang is pictured in Richmond, B.C., on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Jiang spearheaded the creation of the lost Legion branch. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)
Uncovering the past
The revival of Branch No. 9 was spearheaded by Richmond community historian Debbie Jiang.
Digging through archival files, Jiang discovered an old newspaper clipping from the Vancouver Daily Province.
"There was a headline that said 'Japanese charter voted down,'" she said. "I thought that was a very strange headline and thought, 'What are they talking about here?'"

A newspaper clipping from the Vancouver Daily Province shows that the Japanese Canadian legion branch was voted down, despite the promise that it would be reinstated after the Second World War. (Submitted by Debbie Jiang)
Jiang, a former project co-ordinator with Library and Archives Canada, dug a little further.
She said that by going through historical files, she found that in 1942, the president of Branch No. 9, Masumi Mitsui, had surrendered its charter.
"When I found that letter of surrender, it did say that this suspension is only until the end of the war against Japan," Jiang said.
But the Legion denied its reinstatement after the Second World War, she said.

items: Japanese-Canadian WW I veterans, once forgotten, remembered by new plaque

blocks.text: After rediscovering the clipping, Jiang worked to connect with descendants of Branch No. 9 members and uncovered archival documents that convinced the Legion to reopen this forgotten branch.
"We are proud to support the reopening of Japanese Canadian Legion #9 and making right a historical wrong," Bob Underhill, president of the Legion's B.C./Yukon Command, wrote to CBC News.

So far, the branch plans to hold gatherings online as most descendants are scattered across the country, Jiang said. An official reinstatement ceremony is slated for February next year at the Vancouver Japanese Language School.
Dozens have joined and the hope is to continue to grow the membership.

Sgt. Masumi Mitsui, centre, was leader of what was then known as Japanese Branch No. 9, The Canadian Legion, British Empire Service League before it was shut down due to internment in the Second World War. His grandson, David Mitsui, is the branch's new president. (Submitted by David Mitsui)
Descendants of members speak out
Mitsui said it was hard for his grandfather to deal with internment and the closure of the Legion.

"I think all of them felt betrayed after they tried to do an honourable thing," he said. "Then they were, literally, you know, spat upon and denied the opportunity to continue their involvement with the Legion."

He recalled Masumi never attended a public Remembrance Day ceremony after the Second World War, but he would still dress in his uniform, wear his Legion beret, shine his medals and honour his fallen comrades at home.
Yoshihiro Kamachi, whose uncle served in the First World War, is pictured in Vancouver, B.C., on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)
"I've joined because of Otoji," said Yoshihiro Kamachi, who served in the military as a dentist.
His sais his uncle, Otoji Kamachi, was a veteran of battles such as Vimy Ridge, and he was wounded five times.

items: 2 Japanese Canadian heritage boats getting new lease on life in Richmond

blocks.text: About 200 Japanese Canadians from B.C. travelled to Alberta to enlist and fight in the First World War, he said.
"Then in the Second World War, they weren't treated very well," said Kamachi. "Most of them were treated as enemy aliens, and then they were sent to internment camps like everybody else."
Because Otoji was a veteran, authorities asked him to spy on the Japanese Canadians he was interned with, which added to the sense of betrayal, he said.

Bunkichi Hamade, a veteran of the First World War. His descendant, Britt Moberg, says that joining the newly revived Branch No. 9 is a way to heal from the injustices of the past. (Submitted by Britt Moberg)
Kamachi said he hopes the re–establishment of this Legion can help bring some awareness to their story.
The Legion seeks to reconnect with other descendants and grow its membership, which is available to all members of the public. Details can be found by contacting them by email.
"They fought valiantly for Canada and it should be known in history that they did serve well," Kamachi said.

articles.title: Why Danielle Smith wants to give a subsidy to the oilpatch despite near-record profits
articles.summary: The Alberta government is preparing to unveil new subsidies later this month for oil companies to ramp up production to help fill the province’s proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast.

image.caption: The Alberta government is developing a new subsidy aimed at the oilsands sector. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·Analysis
The Alberta government is preparing to unveil new subsidies later this month for oil companies to ramp up production to help fill the province’s proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast.
Oil and gas industry forecast to post revenues of more than $200B this year

The Alberta government is preparing to unveil new subsidies later this month for oil companies to ramp up production in order to help fill the province's proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast.

The incentives would come as the largest oil producers are posting billions of dollars in profits in their latest financial results and the industry as a whole is experiencing one of its most lucrative years over the last decade.

Suncor Energy, Cenovus Energy, Canadian Natural Resources and Imperial Oil posted combined profits of more than $12.5 billion in recent quarterly earnings reports. The Canadian oil and gas industry is forecast to post revenues of more than $200 billion in 2026, according to Studio Energy, after oil prices climbed above $100 US per barrel several times this year amid the U.S.-Iran war.
That's why some industry experts question why new subsidies are needed.
"What kind of incentives does the oil and gas sector really need?" said Janet Annesley, a former executive with Husky Energy and Shell Canada, on CBC Radio's Alberta at Noon.

"They've got money, they're buying back shares, they're flowing lots of dividends to shareholders. So what really more do we Albertans have to do to get them to make investments here and have more projects?"
Premier Danielle Smith, Annesley said, will have to "prosecute the case with Albertans about why we should be giving more incentives to oil companies."
LISTEN | Digging into the Pacific Link pipeline:
West of Centre32:08Pacific Link: A pipeline in whose interest?

Oil production is already at record levels, but with several new and expanded pipeline projects in development, there is uncertainty whether the industry will pump out enough crude to justify beginning construction on the Pacific Link — for which Smith wants construction to begin in fall 2027.
The province is seeking to create an "alternative enhanced royalty structure," according to Smith, to incentivize companies to commit to growing oil production.

"We hope that once that is on the table and they know all of the factors that would go into it, I suspect that you're going to see a lot of interest in being able to fill that pipeline," Smith told journalists in Fort McMurray, Alta., in September.
More oil wanted

The new subsidy is expected to be aimed at the oilsands sector, since that is the source of most oil production in the province and new projects are often large enough to noticeably increase overall production levels.

The Alberta government already provides a financial incentive to oilsands companies to build new projects, since they pay much lower levels of royalties to the government during the first few years of operation.
A view of Suncor's Base Plant oilsands mine. Suncor is one of the companies considering whether to proceed with expanding production in the oilsands. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)
Already, some companies are hinting at potentially moving quicker to build new projects.
Imperial Oil was considering a decision to proceed with its Aspen oilsands project by the end of the decade, but chief executive John Whelan said that could occur sooner.

"We are looking at do we want to bring it forward," he said, during a conference call with analysts on Oct. 30, while acknowledging the company is encouraged by steps taken by the provincial and federal governments to support the sector.
Suncor executives are looking at their growth plans over the next several years and contemplating how they could potentially move faster, if they decide to, said chief executive Rich Kruger.
"We're asking ourselves and doing some preliminary work," he said, during a conference call with analysts on Nov. 4.
"We're all anxiously waiting to hear more from the province on royalties and incentives there. The parties are all sleeves rolled up, meeting endlessly, working hard together."
The Oil Sands Alliance would not comment on the proposed Alberta incentives until an actual announcement is made.
Introducing a deadline

Some oil companies could be hinting at possible growth plans as a way to alert investors and gauge their interest. Despite lucrative oil prices, many investors would rather oil companies continue to produce hefty profits for shareholders, as opposed to spending billions of dollars to invest in new projects.
Many investors are enjoying the robust profits and are reluctant to give up the cash they collect, says Mark Little, the former chief executive of Suncor.
The company leaders are "testing investors' appetite for expansion," said Little, to hear if they will support growth plans or if they warn not to do it.
"To me, the biggest uncertainty on growth isn't the [federal government], it's not the province, it's not money," said Little, "It's whether the investor will support it."
Former Suncor executive Mark Little, pictured in 2022, says the current Alberta royalty system works well. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)
The last large oilsands project to be constructed was nearly a decade ago, which is why Little says it's important for the industry to make investments to ensure the sector's long-term future.
"I almost call it the 'liquidation phase' because all we've been doing is basically producing, spending as little as possible, and handing the cash back to the shareholders," he said.
An aerial view of an oilsands mine north of Fort McMurray, Alta. Oil production continues to increase as companies expand and improve existing facilities. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

The Alberta government's move to introduce a new incentive is "mystifying," said Little, since the current royalty system is already sophisticated, flexible and works well. However, he could see merit in the provincial government introducing a deadline for companies to develop the properties they own.
Production from the oilsands continues to increase as companies invest in expansion projects and find ways to improve existing operations.

Lennie Kaplan, who previously served as a senior manager with the Treasury Board, estimates that some level of incentives are necessary for companies to spend billions of dollars to build new large-scale oilsands projects.
"These projects are very capital intensive," he said, about the level of investment required.

items: Ottawa wants to expand the oilsands, but the industry's wastewater problem will grow with it
First Nations challenging Pacific Link pipeline’s national-interest designation

blocks.text: For the Alberta government to reach its goal of doubling oil production, Kaplan's calculations estimate the government would need to provide $115 billion of incentives between 2027 and 2050, which includes $95 billion of royalty relief and $18 billion of additional construction subsidies. Under that scenario of normal oil prices, as forecast by Alberta Energy, the government would collect an additional $250 billion in royalties.
However, in a scenario with low oil prices, the government would need to provide $240 billion of incentives and yet experience a net fiscal loss of $80 billion.
Kaplan's modelling does account for other considerations, including a rising industrial carbon tax, which he said is important considering the Alberta government still pledges to be net-zero by 2050.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kyle Bakx is a Calgary-based journalist with the network business unit at CBC News. He files stories from across the country and internationally for web, radio, TV and social media platforms. You can email story ideas to kyle.bakx@cbc.ca.
